cases.title: Case 1: Perinatal Loss: Therapeutic Communication After a Stillbirth
cases.short: Perinatal Loss: Therapeutic Communication After a Stillbirth
cases.description: Review the chart and handoff report of a 39-year-old patient who delivered a stillborn son overnight. Decide how to respond verbally and non-verbally as her primary nurse, while still watching for postpartum complications.
objectives: Choose therapeutic verbal responses and avoid communication blocks with a grieving family.
Describe non-verbal behaviors that convey presence and respect.
Recognize physiological cues (bleeding, Rh status) that still need follow-up during bereavement care.
Plan culturally and spiritually responsive care after perinatal loss.
cases.scenario: You are the day-shift nurse on the postpartum unit. Your patient, Hana Kareem, delivered a stillborn son, Yusuf, at 03:12. Review the chart and the night nurse's handoff before you go into the room.

items.q: When you introduce yourself, Hana says: "This is my fault. If I had come in yesterday, Yusuf would be alive." Which response by the nurse is most therapeutic?
items.rationale: Reflecting her feeling and inviting her to say more (an open-ended response) shows acceptance and lets her express guilt, a common part of grief. Telling her not to blame herself is false reassurance that dismisses her feeling; talking about future pregnancies minimizes this loss; referring to the doctor changes the subject from her feelings to facts she is not asking for.
options: "You couldn't have known. Please don't blame yourself."
"You're wondering whether you could have changed what happened. Tell me more about what you are feeling."
"Many women have a healthy baby after a stillbirth."
"Dr. Morgan will explain the cause once the autopsy results are back."

items.q: Which non-verbal behaviors convey presence and respect when you enter Hana's room? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Knocking and introducing yourself, sitting at eye level, tolerating silence, offering touch that the patient accepts, and giving undivided attention convey presence. Standing at the foot of the bed with a chart creates distance; broad smiling can seem out of place in acute grief; hurrying the visit suggests the nurse has no time for her.
options: Knock, pause, and introduce yourself by name and role
Sit at eye level near the head of the bed
Allow periods of silence without filling them
Offer a gentle touch on the arm if she accepts it
Stand at the foot of the bed with the chart open
Smile broadly to lift the mood in the room
Turn off your phone ringer and avoid looking at the clock
Keep the visit short so the couple can rest

items.q: For each statement a nurse might make to Hana and Omar, decide whether it is therapeutic or non-therapeutic.
items.rationale: Naming the baby, offering time with him and asking what the family needs are therapeutic. "At least…", "I know exactly how you feel" and "Everything happens for a reason" are clichés that minimize the loss or assume the nurse understands.
rows: "At least you have a healthy daughter at home."
"You can hold Yusuf again whenever you want. Take as much time as you need."
"What would help your family most right now?"

items.q: Highlight the findings in Hana's chart and handoff that require nursing follow-up during your shift.
items.rationale: A heavy pad with a boggy fundus that has not been reassessed, a falling hemoglobin with a rising heart rate, Rh immune globulin that is still pending, and an unmet urgent spiritual request all need action. Mild cramping relieved by ibuprofen, soft breasts on day 0, a normal temperature and an intact repair are expected findings.
options: Pain 3/10, cramping, relieved by ibuprofen
Pad saturated in about 1 hour at 06:15 with a boggy fundus, not rechecked since
Blood type O negative; cord blood Rh and Kleihauer-Betke pending
Breasts soft, no engorgement yet
Husband asked for an imam and for burial today; spiritual care has not called back
Temperature 37.0 °C
Hemoglobin 10.1 g/dL (11.8 g/dL on admission) with heart rate 92-96
Second-degree repair intact, mild edema

items.q: Complete the nurse's reasoning about the Rh immune globulin.
items.rationale: An Rh-negative, unsensitized mother receives Rh(D) immune globulin within 72 hours when the infant is Rh-positive or the type cannot be determined, as in many stillbirths. It prevents alloimmunization that would threaten a future Rh-positive fetus. The Kleihauer-Betke test measures fetal cells in maternal blood to calculate whether more than one 300 mcg vial is needed.

options: Rh-positive
Rh-negative
not yet known
known to be negative
24 hours
72 hours
7 days
maternal sensitization (antibodies) that could affect a future Rh-positive baby
a transfusion reaction
postpartum hemorrhage
Kleihauer-Betke

items.q: Put these nursing actions for the start of your shift in priority order (first = do first).
items.rationale: Physiological safety comes first: a heavy pad with a boggy fundus that has not been rechecked could signal postpartum hemorrhage. The family's urgent spiritual need is time-sensitive because of burial customs, followed by unhurried time with their son. Engorgement teaching and support group information are important but can happen later in the stay.
options: Give written information about perinatal loss support groups before discharge
Teach comfort measures for breast engorgement, which may begin in 2 to 4 days
Offer the parents time with Yusuf and memory-making options (photos, hand and footprints, a lock of hair) in line with their wishes
Assess fundal tone, lochia and vital signs
Contact spiritual care again and confirm when the imam will come, because the family wishes to bury Yusuf today

items.q: Write what you would say (verbal) and do (non-verbal) during your first two minutes in Hana's room this morning. Include how you would acknowledge Yusuf and how you would combine your physical assessment with emotional support.
items.rationale: Look for: introduction and acknowledgement of the baby by name, presence and silence, open questions, explanation before the fundal check, and an offer of ongoing support. Deduct for false reassurance, clichés or rushing.
items.model: Knock, wait, enter quietly and introduce myself: "Good morning, Hana and Omar. I'm [name], I'll be your nurse today. I'm so sorry about Yusuf." Sit at eye level, keep an open posture, give her my full attention and allow silence. Ask: "How are you doing right now?" and listen. Explain gently before touching: "I need to check your uterus and your bleeding, because you were bleeding more earlier. It may be uncomfortable; I'll be as gentle as I can." Offer to stay with them, and ask what would help most today (seeing Yusuf, an imam, telling their daughter). Avoid clichés and false reassurance.

items.q: Omar asks, "How do we tell our 6-year-old daughter?" and asks for burial "today if we can." Describe two actions you would take for the family's spiritual and cultural needs and one way you would help them prepare to talk with their daughter.
items.rationale: Credit timely escalation of the spiritual care request, asking the family about their own practices, coordinating paperwork for burial customs, and concrete, honest language for a young child.
items.model: Spiritual and cultural: page spiritual care again (or call the on-call imam directly per policy) and give the family a time; ask the family which rituals they want (for example washing the body, prayers) and involve the bereavement coordinator and the provider so that autopsy consent, the death certificate and release of the body are handled quickly enough for burial within 24 hours, respecting that they may decline autopsy. Daughter: offer honest, simple, age-appropriate words ("The baby died. His body stopped working. It is not anyone's fault"), avoid euphemisms like "sleeping", offer child life or social work support and children's books on grief, and invite the daughter to visit if the parents wish.

cases.title: Case 2: Hard News: Responding to a New Lung Cancer Diagnosis
cases.short: Hard News: Responding to a New Lung Cancer Diagnosis
cases.description: A 58-year-old man has just been told he has metastatic lung cancer. Respond therapeutically to his questions, and notice the new physical complaint that could be an oncologic emergency.
objectives: Respond to "Am I going to die?" with honesty, presence and open questions.
Identify the nurse's role after a provider shares bad news.
Recognize the cues of metastatic spinal cord compression and act on them.
Separate expected emotional responses from findings that need urgent escalation.
cases.scenario: It is 14:30. The oncologist has just told Daniel Okafor and his wife that his biopsy shows stage IV lung adenocarcinoma. You are his nurse for the day shift on the medical oncology unit.

items.q: After the oncologist leaves, Daniel looks at you and asks quietly, "Am I going to die?" Which response is best?
items.rationale: Acknowledging the feeling and asking what he understood (an open question) begins an honest conversation, lets the nurse correct misunderstandings and keeps the nurse present. The first response is false reassurance, the second shuts down the conversation, and the last is a cliché that minimizes his fear.
options: "Don't think that way. Lots of people live for years with treatment."
"That's a question for Dr. Raman. I can ask her to come back."
"That is a frightening question. What did you understand from what Dr. Raman told you?"
"Everyone dies eventually. Try to focus on today."

items.q: Which actions are within the nurse's role after the provider has disclosed a serious diagnosis? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Nurses reinforce and clarify information, stay present, communicate the patient's unanswered questions to the team, mobilize the supports he chooses and treat symptoms. Giving prognostic estimates is outside the nurse's role and could be inaccurate; advising secrecy within the family is not patient-centered.
options: Stay with the patient and family and allow silence
Find out what the patient understood and what he wants to know next
Give the patient the expected survival time from the internet
Tell the provider about questions the patient could not ask
Offer to contact the chaplain or other supports the patient chooses
Suggest the family not tell the children until treatment starts
Check for physical symptoms (pain, breathlessness) that add to distress

items.q: Highlight the findings that together suggest a new, urgent problem rather than an expected response to the diagnosis.
items.rationale: Back pain worse lying flat in a patient with a vertebral metastasis, plus new leg weakness and sensory change, constipation and urinary hesitancy, point to metastatic spinal cord compression: an oncologic emergency where delay can mean permanent paralysis. Tearfulness and poor appetite are expected after bad news; SpO₂ 94% and minor streaking are unchanged from earlier.
options: Very quiet and tearful after the diagnosis
Back pain for several days that is worse lying down
PET-CT: metastasis in the T8 vertebral body
Legs feel "heavy and tingly," unsteady when walking
No bowel movement for 3 days and difficulty starting the urine stream
Ate 25% of lunch
SpO₂ 94% on room air
One small streak of blood in the sputum this morning

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Daniel's new findings.
items.rationale: The pattern (back pain worse supine, known T8 metastasis, leg weakness and paresthesia, bowel and bladder changes) is spinal cord compression. The nurse reports it immediately (the provider typically orders dexamethasone and an urgent MRI of the spine) and protects him from falls. Neurological status and retention are the parameters that show progression. Walking risks injury, an enema does not address the cause, and stopping analgesia would leave pain untreated.
actions: Notify the provider now using SBAR and report the new neurological findings
Keep him on bed rest and assist with all mobility until he is evaluated
Encourage him to walk the hallway to build strength
Give a large-volume enema
Hold all opioids

items.q: Daniel's daughter Ada asks you about her father's reactions. Classify each finding as an expected response to the news, or a finding that needs escalation.
items.rationale: Anger, difficulty retaining information and wanting family close are common after bad news. New bilateral numbness and urinary retention suggest cord compression; any statement about ending one's life requires a direct suicide risk assessment and escalation.
rows: Asks "Why me?" and is angry at himself for smoking
Cannot remember what the doctor said about treatment
Tells the nurse he has thought about ending his life rather than "suffering like my father did"
Wants to call his son abroad tonight
Unable to pass urine for 8 hours with lower abdominal fullness

items.q: Complete the SBAR the nurse gives Dr. Raman.
items.rationale: An effective SBAR states the new finding, the relevant background (vertebral metastasis), the nurse's concern and a clear, time-sensitive request. Suspected cord compression needs prompt evaluation; corticosteroids and MRI are usually ordered urgently.
items.text: S: Daniel Okafor in room 14 has new {0} since about noon. B: He has stage IV lung cancer with a metastasis in {1} and back pain that is worse lying down. A: I am concerned about {2}. He has not had a bowel movement in 3 days and had urinary hesitancy. R: I would like you to {3}, and I have kept him {4}.

options: bilateral leg weakness and tingling
nausea
T8
the brain
pneumonia
spinal cord compression
review him in the morning
come and assess him now
on bed rest with assistance
walking in the hallway

items.q: Later Daniel says, "I did this to myself. I smoked for forty years." Write a therapeutic response and explain which technique you used and why.
items.rationale: Credit an empathic reflection or open question plus a correct name and purpose of the technique. Deduct for blaming, false reassurance, or lecturing about smoking.
items.model: Example: "It sounds like you are carrying a lot of guilt right now. Tell me more about what you're feeling." (Reflecting feelings and an open-ended invitation.) This acknowledges his feeling without agreeing or arguing, avoids false reassurance ("It's not your fault") and lets him express guilt, which is a common part of grief, so the nurse can assess his coping.

cases.title: Case 3: Faith, Fasting and Diabetes: Culturally Responsive Teaching Before Ramadan
cases.short: Faith, Fasting and Diabetes: Culturally Responsive Teaching Before Ramadan
cases.description: A 52-year-old man with type 2 diabetes on insulin and a sulfonylurea plans to fast during Ramadan. Assess his risk, respect his decision, and build a safe fasting plan with him.
objectives: Assess the risks of fasting for a person with diabetes using his medications, glucose log and history.
Respect religious practice while giving accurate safety information.
Teach when to check glucose and when to break the fast.
Create an individualized, culturally responsive teaching plan and evaluate understanding with teach-back.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse in a primary care diabetes clinic, three weeks before Ramadan. Khalid Al-Harbi has come for a pre-Ramadan review with the physician and you will do his education.

items.q: Khalid says firmly, "Everyone tells me not to fast. I am going to fast." What is the nurse's best response?
items.rationale: Respecting his autonomy and religious practice while partnering on safety builds trust and makes it more likely he will follow the safety plan. Forbidding fasting or quoting religious exemptions dismisses his values; deferring to the physician avoids the education he needs now.
options: "With your history of low sugars, fasting is not safe for you."
"Fasting is important to you. Let's work out together how you can fast as safely as possible."
"Religious scholars say people with diabetes do not have to fast, so you don't need to."
"I will ask the doctor to talk to you again about the risks."

items.q: Highlight the findings that increase Khalid's risk of harm during fasting.
items.rationale: Sulfonylureas and insulin cause hypoglycemia during fasting; he has had severe hypoglycemia and did not break the fast; his job makes afternoon hypoglycemia dangerous to others; skipping suhoor and not testing increase risk; large carbohydrate-heavy iftars cause hyperglycemia. Stable kidney function, controlled blood pressure and evening walking (after iftar) are not added risks.
options: Takes glimepiride (a sulfonylurea) and insulin glargine
Glucose 52 mg/dL with confusion at the bus depot last Ramadan, and continued fasting at 61 mg/dL
Drives a school bus in the afternoon, near the end of the fasting day
Skips suhoor and believes checking glucose breaks the fast
eGFR 72 mL/min/1.73 m²
Large iftar with sweets, glucose 231-268 mg/dL after iftar
Blood pressure 132/84 mm Hg
Walks after evening prayer

items.q: Complete the rules for breaking the fast that the nurse teaches (international Diabetes and Ramadan guidance).
items.rationale: Guidance from the International Diabetes Federation and the Diabetes and Ramadan Alliance and most Islamic scholars agree that finger-stick testing does not invalidate the fast. The fast should be broken for glucose < 70 mg/dL or > 300 mg/dL, or for symptoms. The physician's plan adds a driving threshold of 90 mg/dL.
items.text: Checking blood glucose with a finger-stick {0}. Khalid must end his fast immediately if his glucose is below {1}, or above {2}, or if he has symptoms of hypoglycemia, dehydration or acute illness. He should check before each driving route and not drive if his glucose is below {3}.

options: does not break the fast
breaks the fast
70 mg/dL (3.9 mmol/L)
100 mg/dL (5.6 mmol/L)
200 mg/dL
300 mg/dL (16.7 mmol/L)
90 mg/dL
140 mg/dL

items.q: Decide whether each part of a Ramadan plan for Khalid is appropriate or not appropriate.
items.rationale: A late suhoor, moving and reducing the sulfonylurea to iftar, a balanced iftar and hydration overnight lower the risk of hypoglycemia and dehydration. Basal insulin is reduced (about 15-30%), not stopped, to avoid hyperglycemia and ketoacidosis. Strenuous exercise near the end of the fast raises hypoglycemia risk; light activity after iftar is preferred.
rows: Eat suhoor as late as possible before dawn, with slowly digested carbohydrate and protein
Take glimepiride 2 mg at iftar instead of 4 mg in the morning
Skip the glargine dose on fasting days
Break the fast at iftar with dates and water, then a balanced meal rather than a large sweet one
Drink most fluids between iftar and suhoor and limit caffeinated tea
Do intense exercise in the afternoon before iftar

items.q: Khalid asks what to do if he feels shaky and sweaty at 15:00 and his glucose is 62 mg/dL. Which instruction is correct?
items.rationale: A glucose below 70 mg/dL requires breaking the fast and treating with the 15-15 rule, then a snack or meal. Waiting risks severe hypoglycemia, and he drives children. Extra metformin does not treat hypoglycemia.
options: Lie down and wait for iftar, which is in 2 hours
Break the fast: take 15 g of fast-acting carbohydrate (for example 150 mL juice or 3-4 glucose tablets), recheck in 15 minutes, then eat a snack or meal
Take a double dose of metformin at iftar to prevent it happening again
Drink water only, because food will break the fast

items.q: Create a culturally responsive teaching plan for Khalid and his wife. Include: (1) a glucose monitoring schedule for a fasting day, (2) two meal or hydration recommendations using foods they named, (3) how you will involve his wife, and (4) two teach-back questions you will ask.
items.rationale: Credit a full monitoring schedule that includes pre-driving checks, culturally specific food advice, meaningful involvement of his wife and open teach-back questions that ask him to explain or demonstrate.
items.model: (1) Monitoring: before suhoor, mid-morning, midday, mid-afternoon (always before the afternoon route), before iftar, 2 hours after iftar, and any time he feels unwell; checking does not break the fast. (2) Meals: eat suhoor shortly before dawn: for example foul (beans), eggs, whole-grain bread or oats, laban, with water, rather than skipping it; break the fast with 1-3 dates and water, then a moderate plate (half vegetables, a quarter rice, a quarter meat), and save fried sambosa and kunafa for small, occasional portions; limit sweetened juice; drink water steadily from iftar to suhoor and reduce strong tea. (3) Wife: include her as the cook and a support, plan suhoor together, teach her the signs of hypoglycemia and how to help, keep glucose tablets in the bus and the home. (4) Teach-back: "Tell me which glucose numbers mean you must break your fast." "Show me what you will do if your glucose is 62 at three o'clock before your bus route." "When will you take your glargine and glimepiride during Ramadan?"

items.q: Two weeks into Ramadan, Khalid tells you by phone that his glucose readings were 84-150 mg/dL during the day, he broke his fast once for a reading of 66, and his post-iftar readings are 190-220 mg/dL. Evaluate the outcome: what went well, what needs follow-up, and what will you report to the physician?
items.rationale: Credit an evaluation that names the met outcomes, identifies post-iftar hyperglycemia as the remaining problem with a likely cause, and gives a concise report for medication review.
items.model: Went well: he is monitoring, his daytime readings are in a safe range, and he broke the fast correctly when below 70, showing understanding of the rules. Follow-up: post-iftar hyperglycemia (190-220) suggests large or carbohydrate-heavy iftar meals or the reduced doses; review his iftar portions and sweets; ask about any symptoms while driving. Report to the physician: the one hypoglycemic episode and its timing, the post-iftar range and the current doses, so the physician can decide whether to adjust (for example the iftar glimepiride or glargine).

cases.title: Case 4: Lost in Translation: Discharge Teaching with an Interpreter
cases.short: Lost in Translation: Discharge Teaching with an Interpreter
cases.description: A 71-year-old Spanish-speaking woman with new atrial fibrillation is going home on warfarin. Use a professional interpreter, find the medication and safety risks in her chart, and confirm understanding with teach-back.
objectives: Use a qualified medical interpreter correctly and explain why family members should not interpret clinical teaching.
Identify drug, herbal and dietary interactions with warfarin.
Teach anticoagulant safety and recognize home risks for bleeding.
Write teach-back questions in plain language.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse discharging Rosa Delgado from the cardiac step-down unit this afternoon. She speaks Spanish and limited English. Her daughter has offered to translate.

items.q: Rosa's daughter offers to translate the discharge teaching when she arrives. What should the nurse do?
items.rationale: Patients with limited English proficiency have the right to a qualified medical interpreter. Family members may omit, soften or misinterpret medical information and the patient may not ask private questions in front of them. The daughter is still an important support and can join the session. Nodding is not evidence of understanding.
options: Accept, because the daughter will help her mother at home
Thank the daughter, use a qualified medical interpreter for the teaching, and invite the daughter to stay and take part
Teach in English slowly with simple words, because Rosa nods and understands some English
Give Rosa the written English discharge instructions to read later

items.q: Which practices are correct when teaching through an interpreter? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Speak to the patient, in short segments, brief the interpreter, use teach-back and document the interpreter used. Interpreters should interpret everything said, not summarize, and the nurse stays responsible for the teaching.
options: Speak directly to Rosa, using "you", and look at her rather than the interpreter
Use short sentences and pause so the interpreter can interpret each part
Ask the interpreter to summarize the teaching in their own words to save time
Brief the interpreter beforehand on the purpose of the session
Ask Rosa to explain the plan back in her own words through the interpreter
Leave the room while the interpreter explains the medications
Document the interpreter's name or ID number

items.q: Highlight the findings that must be addressed before Rosa goes home on warfarin.
items.rationale: NSAIDs such as naproxen and ginkgo increase bleeding risk with warfarin; leafy greens are rich in vitamin K and must be kept consistent, not stopped suddenly; falls while anticoagulated can cause serious bleeding; and apparent agreement in English is not understanding. An INR of 2.4 is in the target range, renal function is normal, and a controlled heart rate is the goal of metoprolol.
options: Takes over-the-counter naproxen 1-2 tablets twice daily for knee pain
Takes ginkgo biloba daily
INR 2.4 this morning
Eats a large spinach and kale salad every day
Lives alone in a two-story house and tripped over a rug last spring
Creatinine 0.9 mg/dL
Nods "yes" to questions in English even when she does not understand
Apical pulse 76, irregular

items.q: Classify each discharge instruction for Rosa as correct or incorrect.
items.rationale: Consistent timing, no double doses, safer analgesics, bleeding precautions and emergency warning signs are correct teaching. Vitamin K intake should be consistent (similar amounts each week), not eliminated, because the dose is adjusted to her usual diet. Regular INR monitoring is required regardless of symptoms.
rows: Take warfarin at the same time every evening; if you miss a dose, do not take two the next day
Stop eating spinach and kale while you take warfarin
Use acetaminophen instead of naproxen for knee pain, and ask before taking any new medicine or supplement
Use a soft toothbrush and an electric razor
You only need an INR test if you notice bleeding
Go to the emergency department for black stools, vomiting blood, a severe headache, or sudden weakness or trouble speaking

items.q: Complete the nurse's explanation of Rosa's INR.
items.rationale: For non-valvular atrial fibrillation the INR target is 2.0-3.0. Low values provide too little protection from embolic stroke; high values increase bleeding risk. Frequent checks are needed early in therapy.
items.text: Rosa's INR is 2.4. For atrial fibrillation the usual target is {0}. An INR below the range means a higher risk of {1}, and an INR above the range means a higher risk of {2}. Her first check after discharge is at the anticoagulation clinic in {3}.

options: bleeding
stroke from a clot
bleeding
stroke from a clot
4 days
4 weeks

items.q: Put these discharge actions in priority order.
items.rationale: An unresolved interaction that increases bleeding risk must be addressed first because it changes the medication plan she is taught. Teaching with teach-back follows. Follow-up INR monitoring and written Spanish materials secure the plan, and the home safety referral reduces fall risk over the coming days.
options: Report the naproxen and ginkgo to the provider and pharmacist and get a plan before discharge
Confirm the home health referral for a home safety and fall-risk evaluation
Teach warfarin safety and bleeding and stroke warning signs through the qualified interpreter, using teach-back
Confirm the anticoagulation clinic appointment and give written instructions in Spanish

items.q: Write three teach-back questions you would ask Rosa (through the interpreter) to confirm she can take warfarin safely at home. Use plain language.
items.rationale: Credit open questions that ask her to explain or show (not yes/no questions) and that cover dosing, interactions and warning signs.
items.model: 1. "Tell me how and when you will take your warfarin each day, and what you will do if you forget a dose." 2. "What will you take now when your knees hurt, and what will you do before you buy any medicine or natural pill?" 3. "Tell me which signs mean you should call the clinic or go to the emergency room." (Also acceptable: "When is your next blood test and where?" or "How much salad and green tea will you have each week?")

cases.title: Case 5: Calm in the Storm: De-escalation in Alcohol Withdrawal
cases.short: Calm in the Storm: De-escalation in Alcohol Withdrawal
cases.description: A 46-year-old man admitted with pancreatitis becomes agitated, tremulous and frightened on day 3. Use de-escalation, recognize alcohol withdrawal delirium, and act on the withdrawal protocol safely.
objectives: Use verbal de-escalation techniques with an agitated, frightened patient.
Recognize the progression of alcohol withdrawal using CIWA-Ar findings and timing.
Take protocol-based actions (benzodiazepine, thiamine, seizure and fall precautions) using the least restrictive approach.
Evaluate the response to treatment.
cases.scenario: It is 06:40 on day 3 of Mark Jensen's admission for acute pancreatitis. A nursing assistant calls you: "Mr. Jensen in 22 is pulling at his IV and yelling about bugs on the wall."

items.q: You enter the room. Mark is standing by the bed, shaking, shouting "Get them off the wall!" What should you say first?
items.rationale: De-escalation starts with a calm introduction, orientation and an offer of safety, using his name, short sentences and a non-threatening tone. Arguing with hallucinations escalates fear; threats provoke aggression; "why" questions feel accusatory and he cannot reason clearly right now.
options: "Mr. Jensen, there are no bugs. You are hallucinating because you are withdrawing from alcohol."
"Mark, I'm [name], your nurse. You're in the hospital and you're safe. I'm here to help you."
"If you don't get back into bed I will have to call security."
"Why are you pulling out your IV?"

items.q: Which de-escalation and safety actions are appropriate now? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Safe distance, an exit route, a calm environment, simple validating language, extra staff and simple choices are core de-escalation steps. Restraints are a last resort that requires a provider order and can worsen agitation in withdrawal; haloperidol is contraindicated by his allergy and does not treat withdrawal.
options: Stand at an angle about two arm's lengths away, between Mark and the door
Reduce noise, turn on soft lighting and turn off the television
Speak slowly in short, simple sentences and acknowledge that he is scared
Apply bilateral wrist restraints immediately to protect the IV
Ask for help so another staff member is present
Offer a simple choice ("Would you like to sit in the chair or on the bed?")
Give haloperidol for the agitation

items.q: For each finding, decide whether it is consistent with progressing alcohol withdrawal or most likely related to something else.
items.rationale: Withdrawal delirium (delirium tremens) typically appears 48-96 hours after the last drink with autonomic hyperactivity, disorientation and hallucinations, as the rising CIWA-Ar shows. The falling lipase reflects improving pancreatitis, and macrocytosis reflects chronic alcohol use and nutritional deficiency rather than acute withdrawal.
rows: Visual hallucinations and disorientation to date

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Mark's situation at 06:45.
items.rationale: Timing, autonomic signs, hallucinations and disorientation indicate alcohol withdrawal delirium, a medical emergency. The protocol directs 4 mg IV lorazepam and notifying the provider when the score is above 20, with seizure and fall precautions. Reassessing the CIWA-Ar and vital signs, including watching for oversedation and respiratory depression, shows whether treatment is working.
actions: Give lorazepam 4 mg IV per protocol and notify the provider (CIWA-Ar > 20)
Maintain seizure and fall precautions with continuous observation
Apply four-point restraints
Give hydromorphone for agitation
Hold all IV fluids
monitors: Heart rate, blood pressure, temperature and respiratory rate (including sedation)

items.q: Complete the nurse's reasoning about thiamine.
items.rationale: Thiamine should be given before or with glucose-containing fluids in people at risk of deficiency; glucose metabolism depletes thiamine and can trigger Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia). The dose is due later, so the nurse clarifies giving it now.
items.text: Mark's IV fluid contains {0}. In a person with chronic alcohol use, glucose increases the body's use of thiamine and can precipitate {1}. The nurse should {2} and watch for confusion, {3}.

options: dextrose
no glucose
Wernicke encephalopathy
hypoglycemia
pancreatitis
ask the provider about giving the thiamine now rather than waiting until 08:00
stop all fluids until 08:00
ataxia and abnormal eye movements
facial flushing

items.q: Mark receives 4 mg of lorazepam IV at 06:55 and another 4 mg at 07:10. At 08:10 he is lying in bed, drowsy but easily wakes to his name, HR 98, RR 16, SpO₂ 96%, mild tremor, CIWA-Ar 9. How should the nurse interpret this?
items.rationale: The score has fallen below 10, vital signs are improving and he wakes easily, so the response is improving. Withdrawal is not over (he is still in the 48-96 hour window), so hourly reassessment continues, as does monitoring of sedation and breathing. Flumazenil can precipitate seizures in benzodiazepine-dependent states and is not indicated when he rouses easily with normal breathing.
options: Treatment failed: give another 4 mg now
Improving: continue hourly CIWA-Ar and vital signs, keep precautions, and watch for oversedation
He is oversedated: give flumazenil immediately
Withdrawal has resolved: stop the CIWA-Ar protocol

items.q: Write the SBAR call you would make to Dr. Petrova at 06:50.
items.rationale: Credit a complete SBAR with the CIWA score and timing, allergy, relevant labs and fluids, an assessment of withdrawal delirium, actions already taken and specific requests, including thiamine timing.
items.model: S: This is [name], RN on 4 West, calling about Mark Jensen in room 22. He is agitated, hallucinating and disoriented with a CIWA-Ar of 26. B: He is day 3 for alcohol pancreatitis, last drink about 52 hours ago, with a history of withdrawal seizures. He had lorazepam 2 mg at 04:05 for a CIWA of 12. He is allergic to haloperidol. Mg 1.4 and K 3.3; thiamine is not due until 08:00 and D5 is running. A: HR 124, BP 168/98, T 38.1, RR 24, SpO₂ 95%. I think he is developing withdrawal delirium. I have given lorazepam 4 mg IV per protocol. R: Please come and see him. I would like orders for giving thiamine now, whether he needs ICU evaluation if he needs repeated doses, and to confirm the magnesium and potassium replacement. Can I read back any orders?

cases.title: Case 6: Spinal Cord Injury: Prioritizing Care for an Adolescent with Tetraplegia
cases.short: Spinal Cord Injury: Prioritizing Care for an Adolescent with Tetraplegia
cases.description: Review the chart and handoff of a 17-year-old with a C6 spinal cord injury in inpatient rehabilitation. List and prioritize her nursing problems, find the concerns in the admission assessment, and respond when she develops a pounding headache.
objectives: Prioritize nursing diagnoses for a patient with a high spinal cord injury.
Identify concerning findings in an initial nursing assessment.
Recognize and treat autonomic dysreflexia in the correct order.
Plan developmentally appropriate teaching for an adolescent and her family.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the pediatric rehabilitation unit. Emily Tran was transferred from the trauma ICU two days ago. Review her chart and handoff; at 14:10 she calls you because "my head is pounding."

items.q: Highlight the findings in Emily's morning assessment that are concerns needing a nursing plan today.
items.rationale: Weak cough with basal crackles (risk of pneumonia), skin breakdown, a delayed bowel program (an autonomic dysreflexia trigger), poor nutrition (which slows wound healing) and the emotional and family adjustment all need active planning. The motor level is unchanged, and a resting BP in the 90s is her baseline after a cervical injury.
options: Fine crackles at both bases, weak cough, incentive spirometry 900 mL
Biceps 4/5 and wrist extension 3/5 (unchanged)
Stage 2 sacral pressure injury and blanchable redness on the heels
No bowel movement for 3 days, abdomen mildly distended
Eats about 50% of meals; albumin 2.9 g/dL; 6 kg weight loss
Heart rate 64, BP 94/60 at rest
Mother does all of her care; Emily asks if she will walk again and worries about friends
Up-to-date immunizations

items.q: Before 14:00, rank Emily's nursing problems from highest to lowest priority.
items.rationale: Airway comes first: weak cough and crackles after a recent tracheostomy put her at risk of pneumonia and respiratory failure. Autonomic dysreflexia is a potentially life-threatening risk with an active trigger. Skin integrity and nutrition are actual physical problems that are not immediately life-threatening, and body image is a psychosocial need addressed alongside them.
options: Impaired skin integrity: stage 2 sacral pressure injury
Disturbed body image related to loss of function and changed appearance
Ineffective airway clearance related to weak cough and basal crackles
Risk for autonomic dysreflexia related to a delayed bladder and bowel program
Imbalanced nutrition: less than body requirements

items.q: At 14:12 Emily says her head is pounding. Highlight the findings that indicate autonomic dysreflexia.
items.rationale: In injuries at or above T6, a noxious stimulus below the injury (here a full bladder) causes uncontrolled sympathetic vasoconstriction (severe hypertension and pale, cool skin below the injury); the body responds above the injury with vasodilation (flushing, sweating, nasal congestion, headache) and reflex bradycardia. Temperature and oxygen saturation are normal.
options: Blood pressure 182/104 mm Hg (baseline about 92/58)
Heart rate 52
Flushing and sweating above the level of injury
Blurred vision and nasal stuffiness
Temperature 37.0 °C
SpO₂ 96%
Bladder scan 850 mL; last catheterization 07:30

items.q: Put the nurse's actions for autonomic dysreflexia in the correct order.
items.rationale: Sitting up and lowering the legs pools blood and lowers BP immediately; tight devices are a common trigger. The bladder (the most common cause, confirmed by the scan) is emptied next with anesthetic jelly to avoid adding a noxious stimulus. BP is monitored closely throughout, and medication is used only if hypertension persists after the cause is removed.
options: Catheterize her bladder using lidocaine jelly
Loosen the abdominal binder, compression stockings and any tight clothing
Recheck her blood pressure every 2 to 5 minutes
If SBP stays above 150 mm Hg after the trigger is removed, give nifedipine as ordered and notify the provider
Sit Emily upright and lower her legs

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Emily at 14:12.
items.rationale: Severe hypertension with bradycardia, symptoms above the injury and an 850 mL bladder identify autonomic dysreflexia. Positioning and emptying the bladder remove the stimulus; lying flat would raise BP further and analgesia does not treat the cause. The bowel is checked only if symptoms continue after the bladder is emptied. Frequent BP checks and recurrence of symptoms show whether the episode is resolving.
actions: Sit her upright with legs lowered and loosen tight devices
Catheterize the bladder using lidocaine jelly
Lay her flat with legs elevated
Give acetaminophen and reassess in 1 hour
Perform a digital rectal check first
monitors: Return of symptoms after the bladder is emptied (headache, flushing)

items.q: Emily's mother insists on doing all of Emily's care, including brushing her hair and feeding her, even though OT is teaching Emily to use a universal cuff. What is the most appropriate nursing approach?
items.rationale: Family-centered care recognizes the mother's distress and need to help while protecting the adolescent's need for autonomy and skill building. Planning together keeps both involved. Excluding the mother or leaving the conflict to Emily is not therapeutic, and complete dependence undermines rehabilitation.
options: Ask the mother to leave during care so Emily can practice
Acknowledge the mother's care, explain Emily's goals for independence, and involve both in planning which tasks Emily does herself
Let the mother continue, because family involvement always helps adolescents
Tell Emily she must insist that her mother stop helping

items.q: Create a teaching plan to prepare Emily and her parents to prevent and manage autonomic dysreflexia at home. Include common triggers, early signs, what to do first, and how the plan respects Emily's developmental stage.
items.rationale: Credit accurate triggers, signs and first actions in the right order, an emergency plan, and teaching that treats Emily as the primary learner and plans for school and social activities.
items.model: Triggers: full bladder (missed or delayed catheterization, blocked catheter), constipation or bowel program problems, pressure on the skin, tight clothing, shoes or devices, ingrown toenails, menstrual cramps, sunburn, sexual activity. Early signs: pounding headache, flushing and sweating above the injury, blurred vision, nasal stuffiness, goose bumps, slow pulse, BP 20-40 mm Hg above baseline. First actions: sit upright and lower legs, loosen clothing, check and empty the bladder, then bowel, check skin; check BP every few minutes; use prescribed medication if BP stays high; call emergency services if it does not resolve; carry a wallet card describing autonomic dysreflexia for emergency staff. Developmental: teach Emily directly as the expert on her body, practice directing others (friends, school nurse) in what to do, use a phone alarm for catheterization, include privacy and peers (for example how to prepare for prom), and teach parents to support rather than take over.

cases.title: Case 7: The Quiet Slide: Recognizing Early Sepsis After Surgery
cases.short: The Quiet Slide: Recognizing Early Sepsis After Surgery
cases.description: On postoperative day 2 after a colectomy, a 63-year-old man is "just a bit off." Connect subtle changes in vital signs, mentation, urine output and labs, escalate, and start the sepsis bundle.
objectives: Recognize early signs of sepsis and use qSOFA and SIRS criteria.
Escalate with the rapid response team and SBAR.
Carry out the first-hour sepsis bundle in a safe order.
Evaluate the response to fluids and recognize septic shock.
cases.scenario: It is 15:30 on postoperative day 2. Ahmed Siddiqui's wife stops you in the hallway: "He isn't himself. He keeps asking what day it is."

items.q: Highlight the findings in the chart and handoff that are early cues of sepsis.
items.rationale: Rising heart and respiratory rates, fever masked earlier by acetaminophen, new confusion, oliguria, leukocytosis with a left shift (bands) and rising creatinine form a pattern of sepsis, here probably from an intra-abdominal source such as an anastomotic leak. Controlled pain, a clean incision and no flatus on day 2 are expected. Note how each cue was explained away separately in the handoff.
options: Heart rate trending 92 → 104 → 118
New disorientation to day (wife says "he isn't himself")
Pain 2-3/10 with the epidural
Urine output about 20 mL/h for 3 hours
WBC 17,800 with 14% bands
Clean, dry incision
Respiratory rate rising to 24
Temperature 38.4 °C after acetaminophen this morning
No flatus on postoperative day 2

items.q: For each finding at 15:35, decide whether it meets a qSOFA criterion.
items.rationale: qSOFA uses three bedside criteria: RR ≥ 22, SBP ≤ 100 mm Hg and altered mentation (GCS < 15). A score of 2 or more identifies a patient with suspected infection at higher risk of poor outcomes. Heart rate, temperature and WBC are SIRS criteria, not qSOFA criteria; both tools support escalation here.

items.q: What is the nurse's priority action now?
items.rationale: With qSOFA 3, the hospital protocol calls for the rapid response team. Sepsis is time-critical: every hour of delay in antibiotics increases mortality. Treating only the fever or waiting masks deterioration; changing the epidural without an order does not address the infection.
options: Give acetaminophen for the fever and recheck in 1 hour
Increase the IV fluid rate to 150 mL/h and call the surgeon in the morning
Activate the rapid response team and stay with the patient
Remove the epidural, because it is causing the low blood pressure

items.q: The rapid response team activates the sepsis order set. Put the nurse's actions in the correct order.
items.rationale: Cultures are drawn before antibiotics so the organism can be identified, without delaying antibiotics beyond the first hour. Antibiotics and fluids are started promptly (often simultaneously through two lines). Reassessment shows whether perfusion improved. Communicating with the family matters but follows the urgent treatment.
options: Draw a lactate level and two sets of blood cultures
Update Mrs. Siddiqui and explain what is happening
Reassess blood pressure, MAP, mental status and urine output after the bolus
Give the ordered fluid bolus of lactated Ringer's
Start the ordered antibiotics (aztreonam and metronidazole, because of the penicillin allergy)

items.q: Complete the nurse's analysis of the medication order set.
items.rationale: Piperacillin is a penicillin. Cultures before antibiotics improve the chance of finding the organism. The Surviving Sepsis bundle gives 30 mL/kg crystalloid for hypotension or lactate ≥ 4 mmol/L: 30 × 84 kg = 2,520 mL.
items.text: The order set lists piperacillin-tazobactam, but Mr. Siddiqui has a {0} allergy, so the nurse gives the alternative regimen. Blood cultures must be drawn {1} the first antibiotic dose. A lactate level of {2} mmol/L or more, or a systolic BP below 90 mm Hg, would trigger the full 30 mL/kg fluid bolus, which for his weight is about {3}.

options: sulfa
penicillin
latex
after
before
840 mL

items.q: Two hours later, after 2.5 L of fluid and antibiotics, the nurse reassesses. For each finding, decide whether it shows improvement, no change or decline.
items.rationale: A MAP below 65 mm Hg despite adequate fluid resuscitation with a rising lactate indicates septic shock. He needs vasopressors (usually norepinephrine) and transfer to intensive care. The lower temperature is a minor improvement and does not offset worsening perfusion.
rows: Oriented to person and place, not day
SpO₂ 92% on 2 L/min (was 93% on room air)

items.q: Look again at the 15:00 handoff. Identify two places where a cue was "explained away," and describe how you would avoid this in your own practice.
items.rationale: Credit two specific examples from the handoff and concrete strategies such as trending, screening tools, reviewing labs and taking family concerns seriously.
items.model: Examples: the rising heart rate was attributed to pain or dehydration without fluid challenge or escalation; the low BP was blamed on the epidural; the confusion was dismissed because he knew where he was; the fever was treated with acetaminophen and then charted as "fine"; labs were not reviewed. To avoid this: look at trends rather than single values, use a structured sepsis screen (qSOFA or the early warning score) every shift, consider the dangerous explanation first (anastomotic leak after bowel surgery), listen to family concerns about mental status, review labs at the start of the shift, and escalate when several small changes occur together.

cases.title: Case 8: Breathless at Night: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure
cases.short: Breathless at Night: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure
cases.description: A 74-year-old man with heart failure is admitted after a family wedding and running out of his diuretic. Prioritize his problems, catch a medication safety issue on day 2, and evaluate his response to diuresis.
objectives: Analyze cues of fluid overload and reduced cardiac output.
Prioritize nursing problems for decompensated heart failure.
Identify medication risks related to electrolyte changes during diuresis.
Evaluate the response to treatment using weights, intake and output, symptoms and labs.
cases.scenario: You are caring for Peter Novak on day 2 of his admission to the cardiac unit. Review the chart before the 09:00 medication pass.

items.q: For each finding, decide whether it is mainly a sign of fluid overload (congestion) or of low cardiac output (poor perfusion).
items.rationale: Congestion causes pulmonary crackles, orthopnea, raised JVP, edema and weight gain. Reduced forward flow causes fatigue, exercise intolerance and reduced kidney perfusion. In practice the two overlap; here the creatinine rise may also reflect diuresis.
rows: Fatigue and dyspnea on minimal exertion
Rising BUN and creatinine with a soft BP

items.q: Rank Mr. Novak's nursing problems this morning from highest to lowest priority.
items.rationale: Breathing comes first (crackles, oxygen requirement). A dangerous rhythm risk from hypokalemia, hypomagnesemia and digoxin toxicity is an immediate threat to circulation. Fluid excess is the underlying problem being treated. Activity tolerance and knowledge needs are important but less urgent today.
options: Risk for decreased cardiac output related to dysrhythmia (HR 56, K 3.1, digoxin level 2.3)
Deficient knowledge: self-management of heart failure
Impaired gas exchange related to pulmonary congestion
Excess fluid volume related to sodium intake and missed diuretic
Activity intolerance

items.q: Highlight the findings that suggest digoxin toxicity.
items.rationale: Gastrointestinal symptoms, visual changes (yellow-green halos), bradycardia and a high level are signs of digoxin toxicity. Hypokalemia and hypomagnesemia from diuresis, and reduced kidney function, increase the risk. Crackles, weight and oxygen saturation relate to heart failure itself.
options: Nausea and poor appetite
"Everything looks a bit yellow"
Apical pulse 56 (was 62-88)
Digoxin level 2.3 ng/mL
Potassium 3.1 mEq/L and magnesium 1.6 mg/dL
Crackles in both lungs
Weight 96.2 kg
SpO₂ 93% on 2 L/min

items.q: For each 09:00 medication, decide what the nurse should do before talking to the provider.
items.rationale: Digoxin is held for an apical pulse below 60 and suspected toxicity. Furosemide would lower the potassium further, so the nurse notifies the provider first (who will usually order potassium and magnesium and may continue diuresis once replacement starts). Metoprolol's hold parameters (HR < 55, SBP < 90) are not met, though the nurse reports the bradycardia. Apixaban and spironolactone (a potassium-sparing diuretic) are appropriate to give.

items.q: Complete the nurse's explanation to a student.
items.rationale: Loop diuretics waste potassium and magnesium. Digoxin competes with potassium at the Na+/K+-ATPase pump, so hypokalemia enhances digoxin binding and toxicity, causing bradycardia, heart block or ventricular dysrhythmias. One kilogram of weight is roughly 1 liter of fluid, so daily weights are the best measure of fluid status.
items.text: Loop diuretics such as furosemide cause loss of {0}. Low potassium {1} the effect of digoxin on the heart, which raises the risk of {2}. A weight loss of 1 kg corresponds to about {3} of fluid.

options: potassium and magnesium
sodium and calcium only
increases
decreases
dangerous dysrhythmias
hypertension
100 mL
1 L
5 L

items.q: On day 3, the nurse evaluates the response to treatment. Classify each finding.
items.rationale: Weight loss, less orthopnea, fewer crackles and a corrected potassium show improvement. A continued rise in creatinine may indicate over-diuresis or worsening renal perfusion and should be reported; persistent edema shows he is still above his dry weight (91 kg).
rows: Weight 94.6 kg (was 96.2 kg yesterday, 98.0 kg on admission)
Sleeps with 1 pillow; no dyspnea at rest

items.q: Mr. Novak's son arrives to discuss discharge. Identify three causes of this admission that can be prevented and write one specific teaching point or plan for each, including how the family can help.
items.rationale: Credit three causes drawn from the chart (missed diuretic, sodium excess, irregular weights) with specific, actionable teaching and a role for the family.
items.model: 1. Running out of furosemide: set up a pharmacy refill reminder or 90-day supply and auto-refill; pill organizer; son checks the supply weekly. 2. High-sodium food at the wedding: teach a 2 g sodium diet, hidden sources (bread, soups, cured meats), plan for special events (small portions, extra weight checks afterward). 3. Not monitoring weight: weigh every morning after voiding, before breakfast, same scale and clothing, record it; call the clinic for a gain of more than 1 kg in a day or 2 kg in a week, or increased swelling or breathlessness. Also: understand fluid restriction, recognize digoxin toxicity symptoms, keep the follow-up appointment within 7 days, and refer to cardiac rehabilitation and home health.

cases.title: Case 9: Fruity Breath: Diabetic Ketoacidosis in a Teenager
cases.short: Fruity Breath: Diabetic Ketoacidosis in a Teenager
cases.description: A 15-year-old with type 1 diabetes stopped his insulin during a stomach virus. Recognize DKA, prioritize fluids, insulin and potassium safely, and watch for cerebral edema.
objectives: Recognize the signs and laboratory pattern of diabetic ketoacidosis.
Explain the relationship between insulin therapy and potassium.
Sequence the initial management of pediatric DKA.
Recognize early signs of cerebral edema.
Teach sick-day rules to an adolescent and parent.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse in the pediatric emergency department and then the pediatric intensive care unit. Ethan Park has just arrived with his mother.

items.q: Highlight the findings that are consistent with diabetic ketoacidosis.
items.rationale: DKA is defined by hyperglycemia, ketosis and a high anion gap metabolic acidosis. Kussmaul respirations are respiratory compensation (low pCO₂), and acetone gives the fruity odor. Polyuria, thirst and weight loss reflect osmotic diuresis and catabolism. A normal SpO₂ and temperature do not support or exclude DKA.
options: Deep, rapid (Kussmaul) breathing at 32/min
Fruity, acetone breath odor
pH 7.11 and bicarbonate 8 mEq/L
Anion gap 26 and beta-hydroxybutyrate 6.8 mmol/L
SpO₂ 99% on room air
Glucose 486 mg/dL with large urine ketones
Temperature 37.4 °C
Polyuria, thirst and 4 kg weight loss

items.q: Complete the nurse's reasoning about potassium.
items.rationale: In DKA a normal or high serum potassium hides a total body deficit. Insulin drives potassium back into cells, causing a rapid fall that can produce dangerous dysrhythmias. Potassium is added once the level is below 5.0 mEq/L and urine output confirms the kidneys can excrete it.
items.text: Ethan's serum potassium is 5.6 mEq/L on arrival, but his total body potassium is {0} because of vomiting and osmotic diuresis. Acidosis and lack of insulin shift potassium {1} the cells. When insulin is started, potassium moves {2} the cells, so the serum potassium will {3}. Potassium is added to the IV fluid once the level is below 5.0 mEq/L and Ethan is {4}.

options: high
low
into
out of
into
out of
rise
fall
passing urine
eating

items.q: Put the initial DKA management in the order the protocol directs.
items.rationale: Fluids restore perfusion first. Insulin is started after the initial fluids, without a bolus in children because a rapid fall in glucose and osmolality increases the risk of cerebral edema. Potassium follows once safe. Dextrose lets insulin continue clearing ketones without hypoglycemia, and subcutaneous insulin is started (with overlap) when the acidosis has resolved.
options: Add dextrose to the fluids when glucose falls below 250-300 mg/dL while continuing insulin
Start the regular insulin infusion at 0.1 unit/kg/h about 1 hour after fluids begin, without an insulin bolus
Add potassium to the IV fluid once K is below 5.0 mEq/L and he is voiding
Establish IV access and give the 10 mL/kg normal saline bolus
Transition to subcutaneous insulin once the acidosis resolves and he can eat

items.q: During treatment, classify each finding as expected progress or a finding to report immediately.
items.rationale: At 14:00 Ethan is improving as expected: glucose falls by about 50-60 mg/dL per hour, acidosis is resolving, potassium is in range on replacement, and a slowly rising sodium is reassuring because it shows osmolality is falling gradually. A very rapid fall in glucose and a new or worsening headache raise concern for cerebral edema; a potassium below 3.0 mEq/L during insulin therapy risks dysrhythmias and usually requires pausing or adjusting insulin while potassium is replaced.
rows: Glucose falling from 486 to 318 mg/dL over 3 hours
Glucose falling by 160 mg/dL in a single hour
A new headache that is getting worse
Potassium 2.9 mEq/L with the insulin infusion running

items.q: At 16:00 Ethan has a new severe headache, vomits, is drowsy (GCS 13) and incontinent, with HR 64 and BP 138/88. Complete the bow-tie.
items.rationale: Headache, vomiting after initial improvement, falling GCS, incontinence, bradycardia and rising BP during DKA treatment are warning signs of cerebral edema, the leading cause of death in pediatric DKA. Treatment is immediate: hyperosmolar therapy, head elevation and fluid reduction under the physician's direction. Neuro status and vital signs show progression. Glucose (246) rules out hypoglycemia.
actions: Call the physician to the bedside immediately and prepare mannitol (or hypertonic saline) as ordered
Elevate the head of the bed and reduce the IV fluid rate as ordered
Give an IV insulin bolus
Give sodium bicarbonate
Encourage oral fluids
monitors: Heart rate and blood pressure (Cushing response)

items.q: Ethan recovers. Which sick-day rules should the nurse teach Ethan and his mother? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Insulin is still needed when ill because stress hormones raise glucose and the body makes ketones without insulin. Frequent glucose and ketone checks, appropriate fluids and early contact with the team prevent DKA. Stopping insulin caused this admission.
options: Never stop basal insulin, even if not eating
Check glucose every 2-4 hours and ketones when glucose is above 250 mg/dL or when vomiting
Drink sugar-free fluids if glucose is high, and fluids with sugar if glucose is low
Stop all insulin when vomiting to prevent hypoglycemia
Call the diabetes team or go to the emergency department for vomiting more than twice, moderate or large ketones, or rapid breathing
Wait 24 hours before checking ketones

items.q: Ethan says he skips school doses because he is embarrassed. Write how you would respond to him and two strategies that respect his development as a teenager.
items.rationale: Credit an empathic, non-judgmental opening and strategies that build autonomy with appropriate supervision, privacy and peer support.
items.model: Response: "It sounds like it has been really hard to manage diabetes at a new school and in front of friends. Can you tell me more about what happens at lunch?" Strategies: involve him as the decision-maker in his plan; arrange a private place to inject (for example the school nurse's office) or discuss with the team options such as an insulin pump or continuous glucose monitor that are more discreet; connect him with a teen diabetes peer group or camp; agree on a shared responsibility plan with his mother (for example she checks his app or meter log each evening rather than doing it for him); involve the psychologist; let him choose whether and how to tell friends.

cases.title: Case 10: Time Is Brain: Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Emergency Department
cases.short: Time Is Brain: Acute Ischemic Stroke in the Emergency Department
cases.description: A 68-year-old woman arrives with sudden right-sided weakness and trouble speaking. Use the last-known-well time, screen for thrombolysis, lower her blood pressure to a safe range, and protect her airway.
objectives: Recognize stroke signs and the importance of the last-known-well time.
Prioritize the first actions in a stroke alert.
Apply blood pressure thresholds before and after thrombolysis.
Screen for contraindications and keep the patient safe (swallow screen, neuro checks).
cases.scenario: You are the emergency department nurse. A stroke alert is called at 09:05 for Margaret O'Neill, who was brought in by ambulance.

items.q: Highlight the findings that are most important for deciding whether Margaret can receive thrombolysis.
items.rationale: Eligibility depends on time from last known well (within 4.5 hours), absence of hemorrhage on CT, blood pressure that can be lowered below 185/110, normal glucose (to exclude a stroke mimic) and no anticoagulant effect or low platelets. Major surgery within 14 days would be a concern, but 4 months ago is not. A mild contrast allergy affects the CTA, not thrombolysis.
options: Last known well 08:10, witnessed by her husband
CT head: no intracranial hemorrhage
Blood pressure 196/102 mm Hg
Takes no anticoagulants; INR 1.0 and platelets 214,000
Mild itching after contrast in the past
Glucose 132 mg/dL
Retired librarian
Right total knee arthroplasty 4 months ago

items.q: Which action has the highest priority when Margaret arrives?
items.rationale: The non-contrast CT is required to exclude hemorrhage before any treatment, and the last-known-well time determines eligibility; in a stroke alert, door-to-CT is targeted within about 20 minutes. Catheters delay care and add bleeding risk after thrombolysis. She stays NPO, and aspirin is contraindicated until hemorrhage is excluded and for 24 hours after thrombolysis.
options: Perform a bedside swallow screen so she can take her morning medications
Confirm the last-known-well time and send her for the non-contrast CT head immediately
Insert an indwelling urinary catheter before imaging
Give aspirin 325 mg because she has stopped her aspirin

items.q: Complete the blood pressure rules for thrombolysis.
items.rationale: Blood pressure above 185/110 increases the risk of hemorrhagic transformation, so it is lowered before thrombolytics. Afterward, the target is below 180/105 with frequent monitoring (every 15 minutes for 2 hours, every 30 minutes for 6 hours, then hourly).
items.text: Before tenecteplase, her blood pressure must be below {0} mm Hg. At 09:32 her BP is 178/98, so the nurse {1}. After thrombolysis, BP is kept below {2} mm Hg and checked every {3} for the first 2 hours.

options: can proceed with the double-checked dose
must give more labetalol first
15 minutes
hour

items.q: Which nursing actions are appropriate during and after tenecteplase? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Thrombolytics are high-alert medications. Frequent neuro checks detect hemorrhagic transformation (headache, nausea, vomiting, worsening deficit, rising BP). Invasive procedures are minimized for 24 hours, antiplatelets are held for 24 hours, and she remains NPO because of dysphagia and aspiration risk. Lying flat with nausea increases aspiration risk.
options: Perform an independent double check of the weight-based dose
Perform neurological checks on the same schedule as the BP checks
Stop and call the stroke team for a severe headache, a new decline in NIHSS, or acute hypertension
Give her home aspirin with sips of water once the dose is given
Avoid arterial punctures, intramuscular injections and nasogastric tubes for 24 hours if possible
Keep her NPO until a swallow screen is passed
Lower the head of the bed flat if she becomes nauseated

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Margaret at 09:20.
items.rationale: Sudden right-sided deficits with aphasia, a normal glucose and a CT without hemorrhage point to a left MCA ischemic stroke, confirmed by CTA. BP is lowered carefully to the threshold (not to normal, which could reduce flow to the penumbra), and she stays NPO. Neuro status and BP are the key parameters. Anticoagulation for atrial fibrillation is delayed after an acute stroke.
conditions: Acute ischemic stroke from left MCA occlusion
actions: Give labetalol as ordered to bring BP below 185/110 before thrombolysis
Keep her NPO until a swallow screen is passed
Give an oral antihypertensive
Start a heparin infusion for atrial fibrillation now
Lower the BP to 120/80 mm Hg quickly

items.q: Margaret becomes frustrated when she cannot get her words out. Describe three communication strategies you would use with her expressive aphasia and how you would support her husband.
items.rationale: Credit strategies suited to expressive aphasia (yes/no questions, time, alternative communication) and specific family support.
items.model: Strategies: speak in short, simple sentences at a normal volume (her comprehension is better than her expression); ask yes/no questions she can answer by nodding or a thumbs-up; give her time and do not finish her sentences unless she wants help; use gestures, pictures or a communication board; reduce background noise; acknowledge the frustration ("I can see how frustrating this is; take your time"). Husband: explain what is happening and the treatment in plain language, keep him updated during thrombectomy, explain that aphasia does not mean confusion, involve him in recognizing her signals, and offer support (social work, chaplain).

cases.title: Case 11: A Dangerous Combination: Acute Kidney Injury and Hyperkalemia
cases.short: A Dangerous Combination: Acute Kidney Injury and Hyperkalemia
cases.description: A 79-year-old man on an ACE inhibitor and spironolactone took ibuprofen for gout during a bout of diarrhea. His potassium is 6.8 with ECG changes. Find the causes, give treatment in the right order, and evaluate the result.
objectives: Identify medication and fluid factors that cause acute kidney injury and hyperkalemia.
Recognize ECG and clinical signs of hyperkalemia.
Explain how each treatment for hyperkalemia works and sequence it.
Monitor for complications of treatment (hypoglycemia) and evaluate outcomes.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the medical admissions unit. George Mitchell has just been admitted from the emergency department. His morning potassium is back.

items.q: Highlight the factors in George's history that contributed to his acute kidney injury or hyperkalemia.
items.rationale: Volume depletion from diarrhea reduces kidney perfusion; NSAIDs constrict the afferent arteriole and ACE inhibitors dilate the efferent arteriole, so together they drop filtration pressure. ACE inhibitors and spironolactone reduce potassium excretion, and salt substitutes contain potassium chloride. Beta blockers can modestly raise potassium but are not a main cause here; his prostate surgery and allopurinol are not contributing.

Ibuprofen 400 mg 3-4 times daily for gout
Lisinopril
Spironolactone
Potassium-based salt substitute
Metoprolol succinate
Transurethral resection of the prostate in 2018
Allopurinol 100 mg daily

items.q: Highlight the findings that are signs of hyperkalemia.
items.rationale: High potassium alters cardiac conduction (peaked T waves, PR prolongation, bradycardia, later widened QRS and sine-wave rhythm) and nerve and muscle function (paresthesias, weakness). The toe is gout, dry mucosa reflects dehydration, and diarrhea is the cause of his volume loss.
options: Tall, peaked T waves
Heart rate 54 and PR interval 0.22 s
Tingling in the fingers
Heavy, weak legs (strength 4/5)
Red, swollen left great toe
Dry mucous membranes
Loose stools

items.q: Match each treatment to how it works.
items.rationale: Calcium protects the myocardium within minutes but does not lower potassium. Insulin and beta-2 agonists drive potassium into cells temporarily (hours). Binders and dialysis (and loop diuretics when the kidneys respond) remove potassium; only these lower total body potassium.

items.q: Put the remaining hyperkalemia treatment steps in order.
items.rationale: Membrane stabilization was done in the ED. Insulin with dextrose works fastest to shift potassium (15-30 minutes) and is followed by albuterol for an additive effect. The binder removes potassium more slowly. Hypoglycemia is the main risk after insulin, especially with kidney injury, so glucose is checked hourly, and potassium and the ECG are rechecked to evaluate the effect.

Recheck glucose every hour for 4-6 hours
Give the first dose of sodium zirconium cyclosilicate
Repeat the potassium level 2 hours after insulin and repeat the ECG
Check the point-of-care glucose, then give regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 50% 25 g

items.q: Two hours after insulin, George is sweaty and shaky, glucose 58 mg/dL, K 5.6 mEq/L, T waves smaller. What should the nurse do?
items.rationale: He is hypoglycemic, a known complication of insulin for hyperkalemia, especially with reduced kidney clearance of insulin; it must be treated and reported. Potassium has improved but is still high and will rebound as the shift wears off, so monitoring and potassium removal continue.
options: Give another 10 units of insulin to lower the potassium further
Treat the hypoglycemia per protocol (for example dextrose IV or 15-20 g oral glucose if he can swallow safely), recheck in 15 minutes and notify the provider
Hold the binder because the potassium is normal
Stop the cardiac monitor because the T waves are better

items.rationale: 0.5 mL/kg/h × 78 kg = 39 mL/h. Sixty mL in 2.25 hours is about 27 mL/h: oliguria. Dark, low-volume urine with a creatinine of 3.2 needs close tracking (a bladder scan excludes retention, relevant with his prostate history); persistent oliguria with refractory hyperkalemia is an indication for dialysis.

items.q: Write discharge teaching for George and his wife to prevent this from happening again. Address pain relief for gout, sick-day rules for his medications, and diet.
items.rationale: Credit avoiding NSAIDs with an alternative, temporary holding of ACE inhibitor and spironolactone during dehydrating illness, stopping the salt substitute, and follow-up blood tests.
items.model: Gout: avoid NSAIDs such as ibuprofen and naproxen because of his kidneys and heart medicines; ask his provider for a safer gout flare plan (for example colchicine at an adjusted dose or a short course of a steroid) and continue allopurinol as prescribed. Sick-day rules: if he has vomiting, diarrhea or cannot drink normally, temporarily stop lisinopril and spironolactone (and any diuretic) and contact his provider, then restart when eating and drinking normally (the "SADMANS" approach). Diet: stop the potassium-based salt substitute, follow the low-potassium guidance he is given while potassium is high, and keep hydrated during illness. Monitoring: blood tests (potassium and creatinine) within about a week after discharge and before restarting medicines; report weakness, palpitations or very low urine output.

cases.title: Case 12: The First Hour: Postpartum Hemorrhage
cases.short: The First Hour: Postpartum Hemorrhage
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: Forty minutes after delivering a 4.3 kg baby, a 31-year-old mother has a boggy uterus and heavy bleeding. Act in the right order, choose uterotonics safely for her history, and evaluate the response.
objectives: Recognize risk factors and early signs of postpartum hemorrhage, including the shock index.
Perform first actions for uterine atony in the correct order.
Select uterotonic medications using contraindications from the chart.
Evaluate response with quantitative blood loss and vital signs.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse in a labor and delivery recovery room. At 15:40 you press on Ana Ferreira's fundus and a gush of blood soaks the underpad.

items.q: Highlight Ana's risk factors for postpartum hemorrhage from uterine atony.
items.rationale: Overdistension of the uterus (large baby), uterine muscle fatigue after a long augmented labor and prolonged pushing, and a full bladder that displaces the uterus all increase the risk of atony. A repaired first-degree tear is a minor source, and asthma and blood type do not increase atony risk (though asthma affects medication choice). Gestational diabetes contributed indirectly through macrosomia.
options: Infant 4.3 kg (macrosomia)
16 hours of oxytocin-augmented labor
Prolonged second stage (2.5 hours)
Full bladder (not voided since 07:00)
First-degree laceration, repaired
Asthma
Blood type A positive
Diet-controlled gestational diabetes

items.q: Complete the nurse's analysis at 15:40.
items.rationale: The obstetric shock index (HR/SBP) above 0.9-1.0 correlates with the need for transfusion; young healthy women may keep a near-normal BP until large losses. Tachycardia and faintness with 900 mL QBL mean she needs the hemorrhage protocol now. A distended bladder pushes the uterus up and to one side and prevents contraction.
items.text: Ana's shock index is heart rate ÷ systolic BP = 118 ÷ 92 = {0}. A shock index above {1} in the postpartum period suggests significant blood loss. Her quantitative blood loss of 900 mL after a vaginal birth {2} the threshold for postpartum hemorrhage protocol activation (more than 500 mL with signs of instability). Her uterus is displaced to the right, which suggests a {3}.

does not meet
full bladder
retained placenta

items.q: Put the nurse's first actions in order.
items.rationale: Fundal massage with lower segment support treats atony immediately, and help must be summoned at once. Increasing oxytocin follows quickly. Emptying the bladder lets the uterus contract. A second IV and crossmatch prepare for fluids and blood, and ongoing quantification guides escalation. In practice the team does several of these at the same time.
options: Empty the bladder with a straight catheter
Weigh all pads and underpads and document the quantitative blood loss
Massage the fundus firmly while supporting the lower uterine segment, and call for help (activate the PPH protocol)
Increase the oxytocin infusion rate per protocol
Insert a second large-bore IV and send blood for crossmatch and CBC

items.q: The provider asks which second-line uterotonic you can safely prepare. For each, decide whether it is safe for Ana or contraindicated.
items.rationale: Methylergonovine is contraindicated in hypertension and preeclampsia, which Ana does not have (her BP is low). Carboprost (a prostaglandin F2-alpha) can cause bronchospasm and is contraindicated in asthma. Misoprostol is safe. Tranexamic acid, an antifibrinolytic, is recommended within 3 hours of birth in postpartum hemorrhage.

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Ana at 15:40.
items.rationale: A boggy, displaced uterus with heavy bleeding and tachycardia with hypotension indicates atony with hypovolemic shock. Massage, oxytocin and bladder emptying address the cause; carboprost is contraindicated by her asthma, and positioning flat (or legs raised) supports blood pressure. Fundal tone, blood loss and hemodynamics show whether treatment is working.
actions: Massage the fundus and increase the oxytocin infusion per protocol
Empty the bladder
Give carboprost 250 mcg IM
Elevate the head of the bed to 60 degrees
Wait 15 minutes and reassess before calling for help
monitors: Fundal tone and quantitative blood loss
Heart rate, blood pressure and shock index

items.q: At 16:10, after massage, catheterization (650 mL urine), increased oxytocin, methylergonovine and tranexamic acid, the nurse reassesses. Classify each finding.
items.rationale: Bleeding has slowed and the uterus is contracting, with improving vital signs. Low urine output after the bladder was emptied and a significant fall in hemoglobin show she still has a volume and oxygen-carrying deficit; she needs ongoing fluid resuscitation, close monitoring and possibly transfusion.
rows: Fundus firm, midline, at the umbilicus
Pad weighed 40 g in the last 15 minutes
Urine output 25 mL in the last 30 minutes after catheterization

items.q: Ana's husband, holding the baby, asks anxiously, "What's happening? Is she going to be okay?" Write what you would say while the team works, and one way to support the family's bonding during the emergency.
items.rationale: Credit honest, simple language without false promises, a plan for updates, and practical support for the father and newborn.
items.model: Example: "Ana is bleeding more than we want after the birth. Her womb needs to tighten, so we are massaging it and giving medicines to help. Several of us are here to take care of her and we will keep you updated. You can stay right here with your son." Keep it brief, honest and calm; designate a team member to update him. Bonding: keep the baby skin to skin with the father, let Ana see and hear the baby if she wishes, and plan breastfeeding as soon as she is stable (which also releases oxytocin).

cases.title: Case 13: Preeclampsia with Severe Features: Magnesium Sulfate Safety
cases.short: Preeclampsia with Severe Features: Magnesium Sulfate Safety
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: A 28-year-old at 34 weeks has severe-range blood pressure, a headache and low platelets. Recognize the severe features, give antihypertensive treatment and magnesium safely, and catch magnesium toxicity.
objectives: Identify severe features of preeclampsia and HELLP warning signs.
Administer and monitor magnesium sulfate and IV antihypertensives safely.
Recognize magnesium toxicity and give the antidote.
Plan seizure precautions and teaching.
cases.scenario: You are the antepartum nurse. Aisha Bello was admitted at 10:00 from the clinic with high blood pressure. It is now 18:00 and the magnesium infusion has run for 7 hours.

items.q: Highlight the findings on admission that are severe features of preeclampsia.
items.rationale: Severe features include systolic BP ≥ 160 or diastolic ≥ 110, persistent cerebral or visual symptoms, platelets below 100,000, liver enzymes twice normal, creatinine above 1.1 mg/dL (or doubling) and pulmonary edema. Proteinuria confirms preeclampsia but its amount is no longer a severe feature. Weight gain and a first pregnancy are risk factors.

Headache unresponsive to acetaminophen
Visual spots (scotomata)
Platelets 92,000/mm³
AST and ALT about twice normal
Protein/creatinine ratio 2.1
Weight gain of 24 kg
First pregnancy

items.q: At 18:00, classify each finding as expected on therapeutic magnesium or a sign of magnesium toxicity.
items.rationale: Flushing, warmth, mild nausea and lethargy, and reduced fetal variability are common at therapeutic levels. Loss of reflexes (about 9-12 mg/dL), respiratory depression (about 12 mg/dL and higher), marked sedation and slurred speech, and a level above the therapeutic range indicate toxicity.
rows: Feeling warm and flushed during the loading dose
Mild nausea and lethargy in the first hours

items.q: Complete the nurse's reasoning about why toxicity developed.
items.rationale: Magnesium is cleared almost entirely by the kidneys. Oliguria (60 mL in 4 hours = 15 mL/h) from worsening preeclampsia reduces clearance, so the same infusion rate produces rising levels. Hourly reflex checks detect toxicity before respiratory depression.

kidneys
15 mL/h
