items.q: Put the nurse's actions at 18:05 in order.
items.rationale: Stopping the source comes first, with an immediate call for help. Breathing is supported while calcium gluconate, the antidote that antagonizes magnesium at the neuromuscular junction, is given slowly. Reassessment shows whether respiratory depression is reversing.
options: Give oxygen and support her breathing (be ready to ventilate)
Recheck respiratory rate, reflexes, level of consciousness and a magnesium level
Stop the magnesium infusion
Call for help and notify the provider
Give calcium gluconate 1 g IV slowly as ordered

items.q: Before the toxicity, at 10:05 Aisha's BP was 168/112 and at 10:20 it was 164/110. Which action did the protocol require?
items.rationale: Severe-range BP confirmed 15 minutes apart is an obstetric emergency (risk of stroke) and needs first-line IV labetalol or hydralazine, or immediate-release oral nifedipine, within 30-60 minutes, with titration every 10-20 minutes. Magnesium prevents seizures but is not an antihypertensive.
options: Recheck the BP in 1 hour
Give IV labetalol within 30-60 minutes of confirmed severe-range BP and repeat BP every 10-15 minutes
Give oral nifedipine extended-release at bedtime
Start magnesium only; it lowers blood pressure

items.q: Which seizure precautions and safety measures belong in Aisha's care? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Precautions aim to prevent injury and maintain an airway: suction, oxygen, padded rails, low bed, reduced stimulation and the antidote ready. During an eclamptic seizure, protect her, position laterally (which also improves uteroplacental flow), give oxygen and time the seizure. Nothing is placed in the mouth and she is never restrained.
options: Suction and oxygen ready at the bedside
Padded side rails and bed in the lowest position
Quiet room with dim lights and limited stimulation
A padded tongue blade at the bedside to insert during a seizure
Calcium gluconate available at the bedside
If a seizure occurs: turn her to her side, protect from injury, give oxygen, note the time and call for help
Restrain her arms during a seizure

items.q: After calcium gluconate and stopping magnesium, Aisha's RR is 16, she is more awake and her reflexes are 1+. The provider plans to restart magnesium at 1 g/h. Describe what you will monitor, how often, and which findings would make you stop the infusion again.
items.rationale: Credit hourly checks of the four key parameters (respirations, reflexes, consciousness, urine output), levels and renal function, fluid limits and clear stop criteria.
items.model: Monitor hourly (or more often at first): respiratory rate, SpO₂, deep tendon reflexes, level of consciousness, urine output (hourly via Foley), BP, lung sounds (crackles suggest pulmonary edema), fluid intake (≤ 100 mL/h total), fetal heart rate; magnesium levels as ordered (for example 4-6 hours after restarting) and renal function. Stop the infusion and notify for: RR < 12, absent reflexes, urine output < 30 mL/h, decreased level of consciousness or slurred speech, SpO₂ falling, magnesium level above the therapeutic range, chest pain or worsening crackles.

cases.title: Case 14: Too Quiet at 03:00: Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression
cases.short: Too Quiet at 03:00: Opioid-Induced Respiratory Depression
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: On the night after surgery, a 58-year-old woman with sleep apnea on a hydromorphone PCA is hard to wake with slow, shallow breathing. Identify the risk factors, rescue her, and prevent recurrence.
objectives: Identify risk factors for opioid-induced respiratory depression.
Use a sedation scale (POSS) to guide opioid administration.
Give naloxone safely and monitor for re-sedation.
Plan multimodal analgesia and monitoring for a high-risk patient.
cases.scenario: You are the night nurse on the surgical unit. At 03:00 you enter Linda Thompson's room for vital signs; she does not wake when you say her name.

items.q: Highlight the factors that increased Linda's risk of opioid-induced respiratory depression.
items.rationale: OSA, obesity, a basal opioid infusion (which bypasses the PCA's safety: a sedated patient cannot press the button), other sedatives (gabapentinoids, antihistamines, hypnotics), PCA by proxy and the first 24 hours of opioid therapy all increase risk. Silencing alarms removed a safety net. Mild postoperative anemia does not cause respiratory depression.

Continuous basal rate added to the PCA
Gabapentin and diphenhydramine (sedating drugs)
Husband pressing the PCA button for her
Zolpidem taken from her purse at 22:30
First 24 hours after surgery
Hemoglobin 10.9 g/dL
Pulse oximeter alarm volume turned down

items.q: What is the nurse's first action at 03:00?
items.rationale: A POSS of 4 with RR 7 and SpO₂ 84% is life-threatening. The nurse stimulates her, gets help, stops the opioid source and supports breathing (head-tilt, jaw thrust, bag-mask if needed) while naloxone is prepared. Oxygen alone can mask hypoventilation. Undiluted 0.4 mg can cause abrupt reversal of analgesia, severe pain, pulmonary edema and hypertension; titrate small doses.
options: Document the POSS score and reassess in 15 minutes
Turn the oxygen up to 6 L/min and leave the PCA running
Try to rouse her with voice and touch, call for help (rapid response), stop the PCA, and support her breathing
Give naloxone 0.4 mg IV undiluted as a rapid push

items.q: Complete the rules for using the POSS.
items.rationale: The Pasero scale is a practical guide: increasing sedation precedes clinically significant respiratory depression. POSS 3 requires stopping or reducing opioids and frequent monitoring; POSS 4 is an emergency.
items.text: POSS 1 (awake and alert) and POSS 2 (slightly drowsy, easily aroused) are {0}. POSS 3 (frequently drowsy, drifts off during conversation) means the nurse should {1}. POSS 4 (minimal or no response) means {2}. Sedation usually occurs {3} respiratory depression, which is why it is checked first.

items.q: Put the rescue actions in order.
items.rationale: Remove the opioid and summon help, then support ventilation (the immediate threat). Naloxone is titrated in small doses to restore breathing without fully reversing analgesia. Naloxone lasts 30-90 minutes, shorter than hydromorphone, so close monitoring for re-sedation is required, and the prescriber must change the plan.

Give dilute naloxone 0.04 mg IV every 2-3 minutes, titrating to RR ≥ 10 and arousal
Notify the surgeon to revise the pain plan

Reassess POSS, RR and SpO₂ every 15 minutes for at least 2-3 hours

items.q: For each finding after naloxone, decide whether it shows the intended response or a problem that needs follow-up.
items.rationale: Restored breathing and arousal, and a moderate rise in HR and BP, are expected. Return of pain needs non-opioid and carefully dosed options. Re-sedation an hour later is expected as naloxone wears off; it requires further naloxone and possibly an infusion, with continuous monitoring.
rows: At 04:10 she is drowsy again, POSS 3, RR 9

items.q: Which measures belong in Linda's revised plan? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Avoiding basal infusions in opioid-naïve and OSA patients, CPAP, capnography (which detects hypoventilation earlier than oximetry, especially on oxygen), multimodal analgesia, PCA teaching and an incident report all reduce risk. Additional sedatives such as zolpidem should be avoided.
options: Remove the basal rate from the PCA
Provide CPAP during sleep (hospital device or bring home CPAP)
Continuous pulse oximetry with capnography and audible alarms
Scheduled non-opioid analgesics (acetaminophen; other options per surgeon)

Teach the patient and husband that only the patient presses the PCA button
Report the event through the safety reporting system

items.q: Write the SBAR you would give the surgeon at 03:20.
items.rationale: Credit the essential facts (POSS, RR, SpO₂), all contributing factors, the response to naloxone, the re-sedation concern and specific requests.
items.model: S: Linda Thompson, POD 1 after TAH-BSO, had opioid-induced respiratory depression at 03:00: POSS 4, RR 7, SpO₂ 84% on 2 L. B: She has OSA without CPAP, a hydromorphone PCA with a basal of 0.2 mg/h added at 20:00, 18 demand doses since 22:00, gabapentin, diphenhydramine, and she took her own zolpidem at 22:30. A: After stopping the PCA and naloxone 0.08 mg IV in two doses, she is POSS 1, RR 16, SpO₂ 95% on 4 L, BP 148/88; pain is now 7/10. I am concerned about re-sedation when naloxone wears off. R: Please come to assess her. I recommend discontinuing the basal rate (or the PCA), a revised multimodal pain plan, a naloxone order for repeat doses or an infusion, CPAP from respiratory therapy, and continuous monitoring with capnography or a step-down bed. Removing her zolpidem from the bedside. Can I read back the orders?

cases.title: Case 15: Fifteen Minutes In: Acute Transfusion Reaction
cases.short: Fifteen Minutes In: Acute Transfusion Reaction
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: A 45-year-old woman with a GI bleed develops chills, fever, back pain and hypotension 15 minutes into a red cell transfusion. Stop the reaction, recognize the type, and find the safety failure.
objectives: Recognize signs of an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.
Carry out the transfusion reaction procedure in order.
Distinguish types of transfusion reactions.
Analyze how a patient identification error happened and how to prevent it.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the medical unit. At 14:30 Farah Haddad calls you: "I feel terrible. I'm freezing and my back hurts."

items.q: Highlight the findings that point to an acute hemolytic transfusion reaction.
items.rationale: An acute hemolytic reaction (usually ABO incompatibility) causes fever, chills, back or flank pain, pain at the infusion site, hypotension, tachycardia and hemoglobinuria within minutes. SpO₂ is near normal, and the pre-transfusion hemoglobin is the reason for transfusion.

Temperature 38.9 °C with rigors
Flank and back pain
BP 86/50 and HR 126
Burning along the vein
Dark red-brown urine
SpO₂ 95% on room air
Hemoglobin 6.9 before the transfusion

items.q: What is the nurse's first action?
items.rationale: Stopping the transfusion limits the amount of incompatible blood: severity relates to the volume infused. The tubing is disconnected so no more blood enters, and the IV is kept open with saline through new tubing. Investigation and notifications follow immediately.
options: Slow the transfusion to 50 mL/h and give acetaminophen
Stop the transfusion immediately and disconnect the blood tubing at the hub
Call the blood bank to ask if the unit was crossmatched
Check the patient's armband against the order

items.q: Put the transfusion reaction procedure in order.
items.rationale: Stop the source, keep IV access for fluids and drugs, and treat the instability. The blood bank needs the bag, tubing and samples to investigate and to make sure the other patient's unit is also stopped. Documentation and incident reporting complete the process.

Collect blood samples and the first voided urine as ordered
Complete documentation and an incident report
Stop the transfusion and disconnect the blood tubing
Assess airway, breathing and vital signs, and call the provider (rapid response for hypotension)
Notify the blood bank and return the bag and tubing with the paperwork

items.q: For each patient, identify the most likely type of transfusion reaction.
items.rationale: Hives alone suggest a mild allergic reaction. Dyspnea with hypertension and crackles in an older patient with heart failure suggests overload. Fever alone with stable hemodynamics fits a febrile non-hemolytic reaction (still stop and evaluate, because early hemolysis can look similar). Pain, hypotension and hemoglobinuria indicate hemolysis.

An 84-year-old with heart failure becomes short of breath with crackles and BP 178/96 near the end of a second unit

items.rationale: A mix-up usually affects two patients. Standard practice requires two-person (or one person plus electronic) verification at the bedside of two identifiers on the armband, the tag and the product.

items.q: Describe what you will monitor for Farah over the next 24 hours after an acute hemolytic reaction, and why.
items.rationale: Credit monitoring for shock, kidney injury (urine output), DIC, hemolysis labs, the ongoing need for compatible blood, and disclosure and support.

cases.title: Case 16: Minutes Matter: Anaphylaxis to an IV Antibiotic
cases.short: Minutes Matter: Anaphylaxis to an IV Antibiotic
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: Five minutes into his first dose of ceftriaxone, a 34-year-old man develops hives, throat tightness, wheezing and hypotension. Give epinephrine first, support him, and plan for a biphasic reaction.
objectives: Recognize anaphylaxis using clinical criteria.
Give intramuscular epinephrine correctly and without delay.
Distinguish first-line from adjunctive treatments.
Monitor for biphasic reactions and teach about epinephrine auto-injectors.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the medical unit. You hung Jamal Washington's first dose of IV ceftriaxone at 10:00. At 10:05 his call light goes on.

items.q: Highlight the findings that together meet the criteria for anaphylaxis.
items.rationale: Anaphylaxis is likely when skin or mucosal involvement develops suddenly with respiratory compromise or hypotension, especially after exposure to a likely allergen. Low-grade fever, leukocytosis and the leg redness are from the cellulitis.
options: Generalized hives and flushing
Lip and tongue swelling with a hoarse voice
Wheeze, RR 28, SpO₂ 89%
BP 82/48 mm Hg
Onset within minutes of a new IV medication
Temperature 37.8 °C
WBC 13,400/mm³
Red skin on the left calf

items.q: After stopping the ceftriaxone, which medication should the nurse give first?
items.rationale: Epinephrine is the only first-line treatment: alpha effects raise blood pressure and reduce airway edema, and beta effects bronchodilate and stabilize mast cells. Antihistamines, corticosteroids and bronchodilators are adjuncts and must never delay epinephrine. Delayed epinephrine is associated with fatal anaphylaxis.

Methylprednisolone 125 mg IV
Epinephrine 0.5 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
Albuterol 2.5 mg nebulized

items.q: Complete the epinephrine administration.
items.rationale: IM epinephrine 0.01 mg/kg (adult 0.3-0.5 mg) into the thigh gives the fastest, most reliable absorption. Repeat every 5-15 minutes as needed. Patients should not stand or sit up suddenly because of the risk of cardiovascular collapse ("empty ventricle"); those in respiratory distress may sit up with legs extended.

items.q: Put the nurse's actions in order.
items.rationale: Remove the trigger and summon help, then give epinephrine without delay. Position and oxygen support perfusion and oxygenation, fluids treat the vasodilatory shock, and adjuncts follow. Continuous reassessment determines whether to repeat epinephrine.
options: Give the adjunct medications ordered (antihistamine, corticosteroid, albuterol)
Give epinephrine 0.5 mg IM in the anterolateral thigh
Stop the ceftriaxone infusion and call for help (rapid response)
Position him flat with legs raised and apply high-flow oxygen
Reassess airway, breathing and blood pressure every 5 minutes
Start a rapid 0.9% sodium chloride bolus as ordered

items.q: Classify each treatment.
items.rationale: Epinephrine is first-line. H1 antihistamines relieve hives and itching, corticosteroids may reduce protracted symptoms, and albuterol treats bronchospasm that persists after epinephrine. The trigger is never restarted.
rows: Continue the ceftriaxone at a slower rate

items.q: By 10:30 Jamal's hives are fading, BP is 118/70, SpO₂ 97% on 2 L/min, and he asks to go home tonight. What should the nurse explain?
items.rationale: Biphasic anaphylaxis can occur hours later. Severe reactions and those needing more than one epinephrine dose warrant longer observation. He should leave with an epinephrine auto-injector, teaching and an allergy referral; ceftriaxone must not be given again.
options: He can go home now because the reaction is over
He needs observation (usually at least 4-6 hours, longer after a severe reaction) because symptoms can return hours later without new exposure (a biphasic reaction)
He will need epinephrine every 4 hours for 24 hours
He should take his next ceftriaxone dose at home

items.q: Before discharge, describe how you will document and communicate the allergy, and what you will teach Jamal about using an epinephrine auto-injector.
items.rationale: Credit a specific allergy record (drug, reaction, date, severity), reporting and referral, correct auto-injector technique and when to call emergency services.
items.model: Documentation: update the allergy record to "ceftriaxone: anaphylaxis (hives, angioedema, bronchospasm, hypotension) on 2026-10-21," keeping the amoxicillin history, so it is visible in all systems; complete an adverse drug reaction report; notify the pharmacist and provider; make sure the discharge summary and his primary care provider are informed; advise a medical alert bracelet; refer to an allergist. Teaching: carry two auto-injectors at all times; signs of anaphylaxis; remove the safety cap, press the tip firmly into the outer thigh (through clothing if necessary) and hold for the time specified for the device; call emergency services after use; a second dose may be needed after 5-15 minutes; lie down with legs raised; check expiry dates; teach his wife; never take ceftriaxone again and tell every provider and pharmacist about this reaction.

cases.title: Case 17: Shaky and Confused: Hypoglycemia in a Hospitalized Older Adult
cases.short: Shaky and Confused: Hypoglycemia in a Hospitalized Older Adult
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: An 81-year-old woman who was NPO for a procedure is found sweaty and confused at 10:15. Treat severe hypoglycemia correctly when she cannot swallow safely, then trace the system causes.
objectives: Recognize hypoglycemia in an older adult, including atypical signs.
Choose the correct treatment based on the ability to swallow and IV access.
Apply the rule of 15 and plan follow-up glucose checks.
Analyze medication and system factors that caused the event.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the medical unit. Dorothy Evans returned from a CT-guided procedure at 09:50. At 10:15 the nursing assistant reports she is "talking nonsense and sweating."

items.q: Highlight the findings that are consistent with hypoglycemia in Dorothy.
items.rationale: Neuroglycopenic signs (confusion, slurred speech, inability to follow commands) and adrenergic signs (sweating) with a glucose of 42 confirm hypoglycemia. Older adults often have fewer warning symptoms, and beta blockers can blunt tremor and tachycardia. Equal grips argue against a stroke, which can look similar, and SpO₂ and temperature are unremarkable.
options: Confusion and slurred speech
Cool, sweaty skin
Glucose 42 mg/dL
Equal hand grips
SpO₂ 95% on 2 L/min
Cannot follow commands reliably
Temperature 36.9 °C

items.q: Dorothy has a patent IV and cannot swallow safely. What should the nurse give?
items.rationale: Oral carbohydrate is unsafe when a patient cannot swallow (aspiration risk). With IV access, dextrose IV works fastest; glucagon IM is the alternative without access, though it may be less effective in some older, poorly nourished patients.
options: 4 ounces (120 mL) of orange juice
Glucose gel squeezed between her cheek and gum
Dextrose 50% IV per the hypoglycemia protocol
Regular insulin to correct the hyperkalemia she may have

items.q: Complete the follow-up plan.
items.rationale: The rule of 15 guides rechecks. A meal or snack prevents recurrence after IV dextrose wears off. Sulfonylureas (especially in kidney disease) and basal insulin can cause prolonged or recurrent hypoglycemia, so frequent monitoring and sometimes a dextrose infusion are needed.
items.text: After the dextrose, the nurse rechecks glucose in {0} and repeats treatment until it is at least {1}. Once she is alert and can swallow, she should eat {2}. Because glipizide and glargine act for many hours and her kidney function is reduced, hypoglycemia may {3}, so glucose is checked every {4}.

options: 15 minutes
1 hour
70 mg/dL
200 mg/dL
a meal or snack with carbohydrate and protein
nothing until the next morning
recur
not recur
1-2 hours for several hours
12 hours

items.q: For each factor, decide whether it contributed to Dorothy's hypoglycemia.
items.rationale: Giving a sulfonylurea while NPO, full basal insulin with no intake, reduced renal clearance, and frailty with low weight all increase hypoglycemia risk. Ceftriaxone does not affect glucose, and holding the mealtime lispro was correct.
rows: Full-dose glargine at 22:00 before an NPO period
eGFR 31 (reduced clearance of sulfonylurea and insulin)
Low body weight and older age

items.q: Which factor most likely delayed recognition of the hypoglycemia after the procedure?
items.rationale: Post-sedation drowsiness can be mistaken for neuroglycopenia, and beta blockers mask tremor and palpitations, so hypoglycemia may be recognized late. A glucose check is indicated for any change in mental status in a patient on insulin or sulfonylureas.
options: Her hearing loss
Drowsiness after midazolam, together with metoprolol blunting the adrenergic warning signs
The thoracentesis caused fluid loss
Her oxygen at 2 L/min

items.q: Identify two system-level causes of this event and recommend one prevention strategy for each. Then write how you would discuss the event with her daughter.
items.rationale: Credit specific system causes from the chart with practical fixes, and an honest, plain-language disclosure.
items.model: System causes: (1) No NPO adjustment of diabetes medications: glipizide stayed active on the MAR and was given; basal insulin was not reduced. Prevention: an NPO order set that automatically holds sulfonylureas and prompts reduction of basal insulin (often by about 20-25%), with pharmacist review. (2) No glucose check after the procedure despite sedation and NPO; the handoff anticipated the problem but did not resolve it. Prevention: glucose every 4-6 hours while NPO and on return from procedures, and a rule to check glucose for any change in mental status. Other acceptable: avoid sulfonylureas in older adults with CKD (Beers criteria) and use basal-bolus insulin instead. Daughter: honest disclosure per policy: "Your mother's blood sugar dropped very low this morning because she received her diabetes medicine while she was fasting. We treated it right away and she is recovering. We are checking her sugar often, and we are reviewing how this happened so it does not happen again." Answer questions and involve her in the plan.

cases.title: Case 18: Every Breath Counts: Asthma Exacerbation in a School-Age Child
cases.short: Every Breath Counts: Asthma Exacerbation in a School-Age Child
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: An 8-year-old arrives in the emergency department with wheezing and retractions after a cold. Assess severity, give treatment in order, recognize the danger of a "quiet chest," and teach an asthma action plan.
objectives: Assess the severity of a pediatric asthma exacerbation.
Sequence emergency treatment (bronchodilators, oxygen, systemic corticosteroids).
Evaluate response and recognize signs of impending respiratory failure.
Teach an asthma action plan and inhaler technique to a child and parent.
cases.scenario: You are the pediatric emergency department nurse. Leo Martinez arrives at 19:40 with his father.

items.q: Highlight the findings that indicate a severe exacerbation on arrival.
items.rationale: Severity is shown by limited speech, accessory muscle use and posture, hypoxemia, a peak flow below 50% of best, and a poor or short response to home albuterol. Low-grade fever reflects the viral trigger.
options: Speaks only 2-3 words at a time
Tripod position and suprasternal retractions with neck muscle use
SpO₂ 89% on room air
Peak flow 48% of personal best
Temperature 37.9 °C
Albuterol at home helped for only about an hour
Eczema history
Wheeze louder on the right

items.q: Put the initial emergency treatment in order.
items.rationale: Correct hypoxemia and give short-acting bronchodilators immediately; systemic corticosteroids are given early because they take hours to work. Reassessment guides escalation such as IV magnesium for a persistent severe exacerbation.
options: Apply oxygen to keep SpO₂ 94-98%
Reassess PRAM, SpO₂ and work of breathing after each treatment
Give oral dexamethasone as ordered
Give the first albuterol-ipratropium nebulizer (repeat every 20 minutes for 3 doses)
Give IV magnesium sulfate if still severe after the first hour

items.q: For each finding during treatment, decide whether it indicates improvement (or an expected drug effect) or worsening.
items.rationale: Better speech, peak flow and less work of breathing show improvement. Tachycardia and tremor are expected side effects of albuterol, not worsening. A "silent chest" with drowsiness means almost no air movement and impending respiratory failure, and a normal or rising CO₂ in a child who is breathing fast suggests fatigue: both are emergencies.
rows: Speaks in full sentences and plays on a tablet
Wheeze no longer heard, with decreased air entry and increasing drowsiness
Heart rate 156 with a mild tremor right after nebulizers
SpO₂ falling to 90% on 2 L/min with rising PaCO₂ (normal or high CO₂ in a tachypneic child)
Retractions decreasing from severe to mild

items.q: Complete the nurse's explanation to Leo's father.
items.rationale: Separating rescue from controller medicines is central to asthma teaching. Inhaled corticosteroids prevent exacerbations only when taken daily. A spacer (valved holding chamber) markedly improves delivery in children.
items.text: Albuterol is a {0} medicine that relaxes the airway muscles within minutes. Fluticasone is a {1} medicine that reduces airway {2} and must be taken {3}. Using the inhaler {4} helps more medicine reach his lungs.

options: rescue (quick-relief)
controller (long-term)
rescue
controller
inflammation
infection
only when wheezing
every day, even when Leo feels well
with a spacer
without a spacer

items.q: Which triggers and contributing factors should the plan address? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Adherence, allergen exposure, tobacco smoke (including third-hand smoke), preventable viral triggers and inhaler technique are modifiable. Physical activity is encouraged for children with well-controlled asthma; exercise-induced symptoms are managed with pre-treatment, not avoidance.
options: Controller inhaler not refilled for a month
New kitten in the home
Father's smoking (smoke on clothes and hands even when outside)
Viral infections: annual influenza vaccine not yet given
Playing soccer, which should be stopped
Albuterol used without a spacer

items.q: At 21:30 Leo has PRAM 2, SpO₂ 96% on room air and PEF 82% of best. What is the most appropriate next step?
items.rationale: He is responding well. Observation after the last bronchodilator confirms that improvement is sustained. Safe discharge needs a written action plan, restarted controller, spacer and technique teaching, a short course of steroid if ordered, and follow-up within a few days.
options: Admit him to the pediatric ICU
Discharge immediately without observation
Continue observation for 1-2 hours after the last albuterol, then discharge with an action plan, controller, spacer and follow-up if he remains stable
Give another three nebulizers to be safe

items.q: Write the key points of a green-yellow-red asthma action plan you would review with Leo and his parents, written so an 8-year-old and his father can follow it.
items.rationale: Credit three zones with Leo's own peak flow numbers, specific medicine actions in each zone, when to seek emergency care, and child-friendly language.
items.model: Green (doing well: breathing easy, no cough or wheeze, can play and sleep, peak flow above 80% of best, about 200 or more): take fluticasone 2 puffs with spacer every morning and night; albuterol 2 puffs 15 minutes before soccer if needed. Yellow (caution: coughing, wheezing, tight chest, waking at night, peak flow 50-80%, about 125-200): take albuterol 2-4 puffs with spacer every 4 hours; keep taking fluticasone; call the doctor if not better in 24 hours or albuterol is needed more often. Red (medical alert: very short of breath, can only say a few words, ribs pulling in, lips blue or grey, albuterol not helping, peak flow below 50%, under 125): take albuterol 4-6 puffs now and call emergency services or go to the emergency department. Also: give copies to school, use a spacer, avoid smoke and keep the kitten out of his bedroom (or rehome if allergy confirmed), get the flu vaccine, follow up with his doctor in 2-3 days.

cases.title: Case 19: Sudden Breathlessness: Pulmonary Embolism After Hip Replacement
cases.short: Sudden Breathlessness: Pulmonary Embolism After Hip Replacement
cases.group: Unit 3 · Taking action in acute situations
cases.description: On postoperative day 3 after a hip replacement, a 66-year-old woman who refused her anticoagulant injections suddenly becomes short of breath. Recognize a pulmonary embolism and act, and plan how the refusal should have been handled.
objectives: Recognize risk factors and signs of venous thromboembolism and pulmonary embolism.
Differentiate pulmonary embolism from other causes of postoperative dyspnea.
Take immediate actions and prepare for diagnostics and anticoagulation.
Address medication refusal with education and escalation.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the orthopedic unit. At 11:10 Helen Carter, walking back from the bathroom, sits on the bed and says, "I can't catch my breath."

items.q: Highlight Helen's risk factors for venous thromboembolism.
items.rationale: Major orthopedic surgery of the hip is among the highest-risk procedures for VTE. Missed prophylaxis, estrogen, obesity, family history and reduced use of mechanical prophylaxis add risk (as do age and varicose veins). Normal kidney function and good pain control are not risk factors.
options: Total hip arthroplasty 3 days ago
Refused enoxaparin for two doses
Oral estrogen therapy
Obesity (BMI 33)
Mother had a DVT
Removing compression stockings
Creatinine 0.8 mg/dL
Pain controlled at 3/10

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Helen at 11:12.
items.rationale: Sudden dyspnea, pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hypoxemia with clear lungs, a swollen calf, distended neck veins and the ECG pattern point to a pulmonary embolism from a DVT. Oxygen, positioning and urgent escalation come first, then diagnostics and anticoagulation. Massaging the calf could dislodge more clot; she is alert with a high respiratory rate, so naloxone is not indicated.
actions: Raise the head of the bed, apply oxygen and call the rapid response team
Prepare for CT pulmonary angiography and anticoagulation as ordered
Massage the right calf to relieve the tightness
Give naloxone
Walk her in the hallway to improve breathing
monitors: SpO₂, respiratory rate and work of breathing
Heart rate and blood pressure (signs of right heart strain or shock)

items.q: For each finding, decide whether it supports a pulmonary embolism, or is more typical of another cause of postoperative dyspnea.
items.rationale: Sudden onset, hypoxemia with clear lungs, pleuritic pain and tachycardia are classic for PE. Cough, fever and crackles suggest pneumonia; slow breathing with pinpoint pupils suggests opioid toxicity; bilateral crackles, weight gain and orthopnea suggest heart failure.
rows: Productive cough with fever 39 °C and crackles
RR 8 with pinpoint pupils and sedation
Bilateral crackles with weight gain and orthopnea

items.q: Put the nurse's actions in order.
items.rationale: Support oxygenation and do not leave a deteriorating patient; call for help; collect data; prepare for diagnosis; then start the ordered treatment. In high-probability PE, anticoagulation often begins before imaging if there is no contraindication.
options: Obtain a full set of vital signs and a 12-lead ECG as ordered
Call the rapid response team
Ensure IV access and prepare her for CT pulmonary angiography
Stay with Helen, raise the head of the bed and apply oxygen
Start anticoagulation as ordered once ordered (for example a heparin infusion or therapeutic low molecular weight heparin)

items.q: What should the nurse have done when Helen refused the enoxaparin on 10/20?
items.rationale: Patients may refuse, but refusal requires an informed decision: the nurse explores the reason, educates about the risk, offers solutions and notifies the provider (as ordered), who may offer an oral alternative such as a direct oral anticoagulant or aspirin per protocol. Giving it without consent is not acceptable.
options: Give it anyway because it is ordered
Document the refusal only; adults may refuse treatment
Explore her reasons, teach why prophylaxis matters after hip surgery, offer alternatives (for example injection site rotation away from the abdomen), and notify the provider of the refusal
Stop the compression stockings as well to keep her comfortable

items.q: Complete the nurse's reflection on the missed cue.
items.rationale: A difference of 3 cm or more in calf circumference is a recognized clinical sign of DVT (part of the Wells criteria). Duplex ultrasound confirms the diagnosis. Attributing a new asymmetric finding to expected postoperative change delayed recognition.
items.text: On 10/20 the physical therapist found Helen's right calf {0} as the left with "tightness." Unilateral calf swelling after hip surgery suggests a {1}, which should be reported so the provider can order a {2}. The night nurse attributed it to {3}.

options: 3 cm larger
the same size
deep vein thrombosis
muscle strain
venous duplex ultrasound
chest X-ray
surgery and physical therapy
infection

items.q: Helen will go home on an anticoagulant for several months. Write four discharge teaching points that address what went wrong in hospital.
items.rationale: Credit teaching that links to her refusal (purpose and adherence), bleeding and clot warning signs, mobility, and the estrogen review.
items.model: 1. Why the anticoagulant matters: she had a clot in her leg that traveled to her lung; the medicine prevents new clots and growth; take every dose, and do not stop without talking to the provider. 2. How to take it (dose, timing, missed-dose rule, injection technique and site rotation if injectable; interactions; tell all providers and dentists). 3. Bleeding precautions and warning signs: black stools, blood in urine, vomiting blood, severe headache, unusual bruising; and signs of a new clot or PE: leg swelling, chest pain, shortness of breath; call emergency services for chest pain or breathlessness. 4. Other prevention: walk regularly, ankle exercises, avoid long periods sitting, wear stockings if prescribed; discuss with her provider whether to continue estrogen therapy; keep follow-up appointments and blood tests.

cases.title: Case 20: Shared Decision-Making in Hypertension and Kidney Disease, Part 1: Understanding the Person
cases.short: Shared Decision-Making in Hypertension and Kidney Disease, Part 1: Understanding the Person
cases.description: A 61-year-old taxi driver has uncontrolled blood pressure and newly diagnosed stage 3b chronic kidney disease. Using the QSEN competency of patient-centered care, uncover his values, preferences, health literacy and barriers before any plan is made.
objectives: Apply the QSEN patient-centered care competency (knowledge, skills and attitudes) to an outpatient encounter.
Identify the patient's values, preferences, beliefs and barriers from the chart and the interview.
Distinguish patient-centered from clinician-centered communication.
Assess health literacy and plan teach-back.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse in a primary care clinic. Samuel Mensah is here for a follow-up after his kidney tests. The nurse practitioner has asked you to do the initial interview and education before she sees him.

items.q: Highlight the statements and findings that reveal Samuel's values, preferences or beliefs (what matters to him).
items.rationale: Values, preferences and beliefs include his goals (avoid dialysis, see his grandson grow up), how he wants information (honest, spoken, with his wife), cultural practices (bitter leaf tea) and practical priorities (his income). Lab values are clinical data, not values. Patient-centered care starts by learning these before making a plan.
options: "I will not go on that machine." (fear of dialysis after watching his brother)
"I want to know the truth, but I want to do something about it."
"I want to see him grow up." (his grandson)
Uses bitter leaf tea, a traditional remedy his mother used
eGFR 38 mL/min/1.73 m²
Prefers spoken information and pictures; his wife reads for him
Potassium 4.9 mEq/L
Needs to keep working 12-hour shifts to earn a living

items.q: Highlight the barriers that explain his uncontrolled blood pressure.
items.rationale: Side effects that clash with his work, cost, a side effect he dislikes, NSAIDs (which raise BP and harm the kidneys), high sodium intake and information he cannot use explain the poor control. His wife's support and not smoking are strengths to build on.
options: Stopped hydrochlorothiazide because he cannot stop for the toilet while driving
Skips olmesartan because it costs $90 a month
Ankle swelling from amlodipine
Daily ibuprofen for back pain
Salty roadside meals and seasoning cubes at home
Written handouts left unread in the car (limited literacy)
Strong family support from his wife
Never smoked

items.q: Classify each nurse statement as patient-centered or clinician-centered.
items.rationale: Patient-centered statements invite his knowledge, routines and preferences and offer choices. Threats, dismissing cultural practices and written-only teaching for a person with limited literacy are clinician-centered and reduce trust and engagement. (The tea should be discussed, not dismissed: ask about it, explain that its effects are not well studied, and consider it alongside medicines.)
rows: "What do you already know about your kidneys and what you would like to know?"
"You need to take all three pills every day or you will end up on dialysis like your brother."
"Tell me about a typical work day, from when you wake up to when you sleep."
"Stop drinking the bitter leaf tea; herbal remedies don't work."
"Would it help to talk about which medicines fit best with your driving schedule?"
"Read this handout tonight and bring your questions next time."

items.q: Which actions reflect the QSEN patient-centered care competency for this visit? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: QSEN patient-centered care recognizes the patient as the source of control and a full partner, respecting values and preferences, involving family, removing barriers to understanding, and communicating them to the team. Limited literacy is not a reason to exclude him from decisions, and withholding information he asked for violates his autonomy.
options: Elicit his values, preferences and expressed needs as part of the interview
Include his wife in teaching, with his permission
Use plain language, pictures and teach-back instead of written handouts alone
Communicate his priorities (work schedule, cost, fear of dialysis) to the nurse practitioner
Decide the medication changes for him, because his literacy is limited
Respect his right to know the truth about his kidney disease, and give information at the pace he chooses
Avoid mentioning dialysis so he does not get upset

items.q: Complete the nurse's summary of his kidney disease, in the plain language the nurse will use.
items.rationale: An eGFR of 38 is roughly 38% of normal function. Albuminuria indicates damage and higher risk of progression. Blood pressure control (often with an ACE inhibitor or ARB, and an SGLT2 inhibitor for many people with CKD) and avoiding NSAIDs slow progression; acetaminophen is preferred for pain. Honest, hopeful framing matches his wish to know the truth and act.
items.text: Samuel's eGFR has fallen from 56 to 38 in one year, which means his kidneys are working at about {0} of normal. Protein (albumin) in his urine shows {1}. The two things that most protect his kidneys are controlling his {2} and avoiding medicines such as {3}. With good control, many people {4}.

options: a little more than a third
three quarters
kidney damage
dehydration
blood pressure
cholesterol
ibuprofen
acetaminophen
slow the disease so they never need dialysis
always need dialysis within a year

items.q: Which teach-back question is most effective for Samuel?
items.rationale: Teach-back checks the nurse's explanation, not the patient, and asks him to explain in his own words. Yes/no questions do not reveal understanding, and asking him to read a handout is inappropriate given his limited literacy.
options: "Do you understand why the pills are important?"
"Any questions?"
"I want to be sure I explained it well. Can you tell me, in your own words, what you will do for your back pain instead of ibuprofen?"
"Read back to me the instructions on this handout."

items.q: Using an Ask-Tell-Ask approach, write three questions you would ask Samuel at the start of the next visit and explain what each question helps you learn.
items.rationale: Credit open questions that uncover values, routines, barriers and goals, with a clear explanation of purpose, and use of the Ask-Tell-Ask sequence.
items.model: 1. Ask: "What worries you most about your kidneys and your blood pressure?" (his priorities and fears, such as dialysis, so teaching addresses them). 2. Ask: "Walk me through how you take your medicines on a work day and a day off. What gets in the way?" (actual behavior and barriers: toilet access, cost, side effects, timing). 3. Ask: "What would you like your health to let you do in the next few years?" (goals: seeing his grandson grow, keep working). Then Tell: share one or two key facts in plain language, and Ask again: "What do you think about that? How could that work with your driving?" Other acceptable questions: "What does your wife think about your health plan?", "How do you feel about the bitter leaf tea and the pills together?"

cases.title: Case 21: Shared Decision-Making in Hypertension and Kidney Disease, Part 2: Building the Plan Together
cases.short: Shared Decision-Making in Hypertension and Kidney Disease, Part 2: Building the Plan Together
cases.description: Return to Samuel Mensah's chart. Recreate his encounter with the health care team using a patient-centered approach: weigh options against his priorities, write SMART goals with him, and evaluate the plan at follow-up.
objectives: Use the SHARE approach to shared decision-making.
Match treatment options to the patient's priorities and constraints.
Write patient-centered SMART goals.
Recreate a patient-centered encounter and evaluate outcomes at follow-up.
cases.scenario: This is Part 2 of Samuel Mensah's case. Review his chart again (the same patient as Part 1). The nurse practitioner has three options she could offer, and wants you and Samuel to build the plan together. Three months later he returns for follow-up: home BP average 138/86, takes his medicines 6 days of 7, eGFR 37, still eats roadside meals 4 days a week, has stopped ibuprofen, and uses the tea "only on Sundays."

items.q: Put the steps of the SHARE approach to shared decision-making in order.
items.rationale: The AHRQ SHARE approach: Seek participation, Help explore options, Assess values and preferences, Reach a decision, Evaluate the decision. Each step keeps the patient as a partner.
options: Evaluate the decision together at follow-up
Reach a decision with him
Seek Samuel's participation: explain that there is a choice to make and that his view matters
Assess his values and preferences: what matters most to him
Help him explore and compare the treatment options, with benefits and harms in plain language

items.q: For each option the team could offer, decide whether it fits Samuel's stated priorities and constraints (work, cost, side effects, kidney protection).
items.rationale: Low-cost generics, timing a diuretic around his work, kidney-safe pain relief and addressing side effects all fit what he told the team. Morning diuretics before driving, expensive add-ons and ignoring side effects repeat the reasons his plan failed. (A dose reduction of amlodipine or a different agent is a prescriber decision; the nurse brings the concern forward.)
rows: Switch brand olmesartan to a generic ARB (for example losartan) that costs about $4-10 per month
Restart hydrochlorothiazide 25 mg every morning before a 12-hour shift
Take a once-daily diuretic in the evening after his shift, or on days off, if a diuretic is needed (per prescriber)
Add a fourth brand-name medicine with no generic
Replace ibuprofen with acetaminophen and stretching breaks, plus a lumbar cushion for the taxi
Continue amlodipine 10 mg unchanged despite the ankle swelling, without discussing it

items.q: Samuel chooses to work on salt. Which goals are written in a SMART (specific, measurable, achievable, relevant, time-bound) way? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: SMART goals say exactly what, how much and by when, are realistic for his life, and matter to him. "Eat healthier" is vague, and "never eat salt again" is unrealistic and sets him up to fail.
options: "For the next 4 weeks, on work days I will bring the lunch Abena packs instead of buying roadside soup, at least 4 days a week."
"I will eat healthier."
"Starting this week, Abena will use half a seasoning cube instead of a whole one when she cooks, and we will check my BP at the pharmacy every Sunday."
"I will never eat salt again."
"By my visit in 3 months, my average home BP will be below 140/90."

items.q: At the 3-month visit (see the scenario), evaluate each outcome.
items.rationale: BP, adherence and NSAID avoidance are improving, and a stable eGFR shows the kidneys have not declined further. The salt goal is not met: explore what got in the way (for example, his wife's evening work) and adjust it with him rather than repeating the same advice.
rows: Home BP average 138/86 mm Hg (was about 157/95)
Roadside meals 4 days a week (goal: packed lunch 4 days)

items.q: Samuel says, "I didn't manage the packed lunches. Abena works evenings and is too tired." What is the best patient-centered response?
items.rationale: Acknowledging his honesty and problem-solving with him respects his circumstances and keeps him engaged. Blame, threats and placing responsibility on his wife are not patient-centered.
options: "You need to try harder; salt is damaging your kidneys."
"Thank you for telling me. Let's think about what could work on your work days. Which roadside foods do you enjoy that might have less salt, or could you prepare something on Sundays for the week?"
"Then we will have to add another blood pressure pill."
"Your wife should make the time; it's important."

items.q: Recreate Samuel's visit as a patient-centered encounter. Write a short script (8-12 lines of dialogue) between the nurse, Samuel and his wife Abena that shows: inviting participation, exploring at least two options, checking his values, reaching a decision together, and teach-back.
items.rationale: Credit dialogue that invites participation, presents at least two options in plain language, asks about values, includes his wife, reaches a decision Samuel agrees to, uses teach-back, and sets a follow-up.
items.model: Nurse: "Mr. Mensah, Mrs. Mensah, thank you for coming in together. Your blood pressure is still high and your kidney test shows some damage. There are a few ways we could change your plan, and your opinion is important. Would it be okay to talk them through?" Samuel: "Yes. Tell me straight." Nurse: "What matters most to you in this plan?" Samuel: "No dialysis. And I must drive." Nurse: "One option is to switch your expensive pill to a cheaper one that also protects the kidneys. Another is to take the water pill after your shift instead of the morning. A third is to change your back pain medicine, because ibuprofen can hurt the kidneys." Abena: "The cheaper pill would help us." Samuel: "And the water pill at night, I can do that." Nurse: "What about the ibuprofen?" Samuel: "I can try the other medicine and stop for stretches." Nurse: "So the plan is: the new cheaper pill every morning, the water pill after work, acetaminophen for your back, and a BP check every Sunday. To make sure I explained it well, can you tell me what you will take tomorrow and when?" Samuel explains correctly. Nurse: "Good. We will check how it is going in 3 months, and you can call me before then."

cases.title: Case 22: A New Ileostomy: Teaching Self-Care Before Discharge
cases.short: A New Ileostomy: Teaching Self-Care Before Discharge
cases.description: A 41-year-old woman with Crohn's disease has a new ileostomy. Assess the stoma, notice the early signs of dehydration from high output, and plan teaching that addresses her readiness and her body image.
objectives: Distinguish expected from abnormal stoma and peristomal findings.
Recognize high ileostomy output and dehydration.
Sequence ostomy teaching based on readiness to learn.
Respond therapeutically to body image and intimacy concerns.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the colorectal surgery unit on postoperative day 4. Megan O'Brien is scheduled to go home in two days.

items.q: Classify each stoma or peristomal finding as expected or needing action.
items.rationale: A healthy stoma is red and moist and bleeds slightly when touched; an ileostomy should protrude about 2 cm so output goes into the pouch. Peristomal skin should look like the rest of the abdomen. A wafer opening that is too large exposes skin to caustic ileal output; it should be cut about 1-2 mm larger than the stoma. A dusky or black stoma suggests ischemia and must be reported immediately.
rows: Slight spotting of blood when the stoma is cleaned
Stoma budded about 2 cm above the skin
Red, moist, denuded skin at 5-7 o'clock under a leaking wafer edge
Wafer opening cut to 38 mm for a 30 mm stoma
A dusky purple or black stoma (if it occurred)

items.q: Highlight the findings that show Megan is becoming dehydrated from high ileostomy output.
items.rationale: Output above about 1.5 L/day, low urine output, orthostatic changes, rising creatinine and electrolyte losses indicate dehydration and acute kidney injury. Drinking large amounts of plain water (hypotonic) can worsen sodium loss from the ileostomy; oral rehydration solutions are preferred. Stoma size and temperature are not signs of dehydration.
options: Ileostomy output 2,300 mL in 24 hours
Thirst, dry mucous membranes, dark urine of 300 mL in 12 hours
Orthostatic drop in BP with heart rate 98 → 122 and lightheadedness
Creatinine 0.7 → 1.3 mg/dL and BUN 29 mg/dL
Sodium 131, potassium 3.3, magnesium 1.5
Stoma 30 mm, round
Temperature 37.0 °C
Drinking large amounts of plain water

items.q: Complete the nurse's plan for high output.
items.rationale: High-output ileostomy causes sodium, water, potassium and magnesium loss. Oral rehydration solutions replace sodium better than water or most sports drinks. Thickening foods help; high-fiber raw vegetables and popcorn can also cause blockage early after surgery. Antimotility drugs taken 30-60 minutes before meals reduce output.
items.text: The nurse notifies the surgeon because output is above {0} per day and Megan shows signs of dehydration. Instead of large amounts of plain water, she should drink an {1}, and foods such as {2} can thicken output. The surgeon may order {3} and IV fluids with electrolyte replacement.

options: 500 mL
oral rehydration solution with sodium
unsweetened tea
bananas, white rice, applesauce and potatoes
raw vegetables and popcorn
loperamide taken before meals
a laxative

items.q: Megan is tearful and has not yet looked at her stoma. Put these teaching steps in the order that best matches her readiness to learn.
items.rationale: Emotional readiness comes first; she cannot learn while overwhelmed. Looking at the stoma is the first step toward acceptance, followed by tasks that build confidence from simple (emptying) to complex (wafer sizing and full changes) and finally lifestyle adaptation.
options: Acknowledge her feelings and explore what worries her most
Teach measuring the stoma and cutting the wafer correctly to protect her skin
Teach a full pouch change, then managing travel and work as a flight attendant
Have her empty the pouch herself (a task she is already starting)
Have her look at the stoma during a pouch change, at her own pace

items.q: Megan says, "My husband won't want to be close to me with this bag." What is the most therapeutic response?
items.rationale: Reflecting the feeling and inviting more opens a conversation about body image and intimacy. Reassurance, generalizing and jumping to practical products dismiss her concern (pouch covers may help later, once she has expressed her feelings). The nurse can also offer to include her husband and an ostomy visitor from a peer association.
options: "I'm sure your husband will love you just the same."
"It sounds like you're worried about how the ostomy will affect your relationship. Can you tell me more about that?"
"Lots of people have ostomies; you'll get used to it."
"You can buy pouch covers that look nicer."

items.q: Which teaching points are correct for Megan's discharge? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Emptying before the pouch is heavy prevents leaks; chewing well and gradual fiber prevent food blockage; the stoma shrinks for weeks, so the wafer must be resized; no output with cramping suggests obstruction; and absorption of some tablets is reduced with an ileostomy. People with ostomies can swim (with a secure seal). Alcohol damages peristomal skin; warm water is used.
options: Empty the pouch when it is one-third to one-half full
Chew food well and introduce high-fiber foods gradually to avoid blockage
Measure the stoma weekly for the first 6-8 weeks, because it shrinks as swelling goes down
Swimming is no longer possible
Call the surgeon for no output for 4-6 hours with cramping and nausea, or signs of dehydration
Use alcohol wipes on the skin around the stoma each day
Ask the pharmacist before new medicines; extended-release and enteric-coated tablets may not be absorbed

items.q: Write two teach-back requests you would use before discharge, and describe one observable sign that Megan is adapting to her body image change.
items.rationale: Credit demonstration-based teach-back on a critical skill and on dehydration, and a concrete, observable behavior showing adaptation.
items.model: Teach-back: "Show me how you measure your stoma and cut the wafer." "Tell me which signs mean you are getting dehydrated and what you will drink." (Also acceptable: "What will you do if the wafer starts to leak at the bottom edge?") Signs of adaptation: she looks at and touches the stoma, performs care without turning away, uses the word "stoma" or names it, asks about clothing, swimming or intimacy, involves her husband, or plans her return to work.

cases.title: Case 23: Too Many Pills: Polypharmacy and Falls in an Older Adult
cases.short: Too Many Pills: Polypharmacy and Falls in an Older Adult
cases.description: An 84-year-old woman admitted after a fall takes 13 medications. Find the medicines that raise her fall risk, interpret orthostatic vital signs and her low sodium, and lead a patient-centered deprescribing conversation.
objectives: Identify potentially inappropriate medications for older adults (Beers Criteria).
Interpret orthostatic vital signs and medication-related hyponatremia.
Carry out medication reconciliation.
Plan fall prevention and a deprescribing conversation that respects the patient's priorities.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the acute care for elders unit. Edith Kowalski was admitted last night after a fall at home. Her daughter brought all her pill bottles in a bag.

items.q: Highlight the home medications that are on the Beers Criteria list of potentially inappropriate medications for older adults (or should be avoided in her situation).
items.rationale: Z-drug hypnotics (falls, fractures, delirium), first-generation antihistamines and oxybutynin (strongly anticholinergic: confusion, falls, constipation, urinary retention), glyburide (prolonged hypoglycemia, especially with reduced kidney function) and long-term proton pump inhibitors beyond 8 weeks without a clear indication (C. difficile, bone loss, B12 deficiency) are listed. Amlodipine, alendronate and acetaminophen are appropriate for her.
options: Zolpidem 10 mg
Diphenhydramine ("PM" pain reliever)
Oxybutynin immediate-release
Glyburide
Amlodipine
Alendronate
Omeprazole for 8 years without a clear ongoing indication
Acetaminophen

items.q: Interpret Edith's orthostatic vital signs.
items.rationale: Standard criteria are a fall of ≥ 20 mm Hg systolic or ≥ 10 mm Hg diastolic within 3 minutes of standing, or symptoms. A blunted heart rate response is common in older adults and in neuropathy (her diabetic neuropathy) and suggests neurogenic causes alongside medication effects.
items.text: Orthostatic hypotension is a drop in systolic BP of at least {0} or diastolic BP of at least {1} within 3 minutes of standing. Edith's systolic BP fell from 146 to 118 mm Hg, a drop of {2} mm Hg, so her test is {3}. Her heart rate rose only 8 beats, which may reflect {4}.

options: 20 mm Hg
5 mm Hg
10 mm Hg
30 mm Hg
positive
negative
age and autonomic dysfunction
dehydration only

items.q: For each medication, choose its main contribution to Edith's fall.
items.rationale: Sedative-hypnotics, anticholinergics and gabapentin cause drowsiness and confusion. A bedtime diuretic makes her get up at night; combined antihypertensives cause orthostatic hypotension. Glyburide accumulates with reduced kidney function (her morning glucose is 68). SSRIs can cause SIADH, worsened by diuretics, and hyponatremia increases falls even when mild.
cols: Low blood pressure or nighttime urination

items.q: Put the steps of medication reconciliation in order.
items.rationale: Reconciliation starts with an accurate list (including how she really takes medicines, such as furosemide at bedtime), then comparison, clinical review, shared decisions, and communication of a single accurate list across transitions.
options: Review each medicine for indication, benefit, harm and Beers Criteria with the pharmacist and physician
Collect the best possible medication history: every bottle in the bag, over-the-counter and internet products, and how she actually takes each one
Compare the list with the admission orders and other prescribers' records to find discrepancies
Communicate one updated list to Edith, her daughter, her primary care provider and her pharmacy at discharge
Discuss proposed changes with Edith and her daughter and agree on a plan

items.q: Which fall-prevention measures fit Edith's risks and her goal of going home? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Toileting schedules, a commode or downstairs bedroom, slow position changes, strength and balance training, home modification and changing diuretic timing target her specific risks. Restraints, including raised bed rails used to prevent getting up, increase injury and delirium and are avoided.
options: Scheduled toileting, including before bed and during the night
A bedside commode or moving her bed downstairs near the bathroom at home
Teach her to sit on the edge of the bed for a minute before standing
Physical therapy for strength and balance, and a walker if recommended
Bed rails up and a lap belt in the chair
Home safety assessment (night lights, remove rugs, grab bars)
Discuss with her provider moving furosemide to the morning or stopping it

items.q: Edith says, "I've taken my sleeping pill for 15 years. I can't sleep without it." What is the best response?
items.rationale: Deprescribing is most successful when it is a shared decision: acknowledge her concern, connect to her goal (staying safely at home), offer alternatives (sleep hygiene, cognitive behavioral therapy for insomnia), and plan a gradual taper (abrupt stopping can cause rebound insomnia). Forcing, deferring or simply continuing are not patient-centered.
options: "You must stop it today. It caused your fall."
"It sounds like sleep is really important to you. Could we talk about ways to sleep well that are safer, and how we could slowly reduce the pill with your doctor?"
"The doctor has already decided to stop it."
"Then you should keep taking it."

items.q: Edith's main goal is to stay in her own home with her cat. Write how you would connect each of three medication changes to that goal when you explain the plan to Edith and her daughter.
items.rationale: Credit three specific, accurate changes from the chart, each explained in plain language and linked to her goal, with a role for her daughter.
items.model: Example: 1. Taking the water pill in the morning instead of bedtime: "You won't need to get up as often at night, which is when you fell, so you can stay safe at home." 2. Slowly cutting down and then stopping the PM pill and the sleeping pill, with other ways to sleep: "These pills make you drowsy and unsteady at night. Feeling clearer and steadier will help you manage on your own with your cat." 3. Changing glyburide to a safer diabetes medicine (or stopping it, since her sugar is low): "Your sugar has been too low, which can make you dizzy and fall. A gentler plan protects you so you can keep living independently." Also acceptable: reviewing oxybutynin, omeprazole or ginkgo, a single pill organizer filled by her daughter, and one pharmacy.

cases.title: Case 24: Yellow on Day 3: Newborn Jaundice and Breastfeeding Support
cases.short: Yellow on Day 3: Newborn Jaundice and Breastfeeding Support
cases.description: A 3-day-old exclusively breastfed newborn has rising bilirubin, 9% weight loss and few wet diapers, and his first-time mother has sore nipples. Interpret the findings, deliver phototherapy safely, and support breastfeeding.
objectives: Distinguish physiologic from pathologic jaundice and identify risk factors.
Recognize inadequate breastfeeding intake in a newborn.
Provide safe phototherapy care.
Teach and support breastfeeding with the mother as a partner.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the mother-baby unit. Baby boy Okoro is 70 hours old. His mother, Chioma, and father, Emeka, are rooming in.

items.q: Highlight the findings that increase this baby's risk of significant hyperbilirubinemia.
items.rationale: Isoimmune hemolytic disease (DAT positive) is a neurotoxicity risk factor that lowers the treatment threshold. Lower gestational age (under 39-40 weeks), suboptimal breastfeeding with poor intake (which slows bilirubin excretion in stool), significant weight loss and family history all increase risk. Cesarean birth, vaccination and good Apgars do not.
options: Mother O positive, infant A positive, DAT positive (ABO isoimmune hemolysis)
Gestational age 38 weeks
Exclusively breastfed with suboptimal intake (6 short feeds in 24 hours)
9% weight loss with 3 wet diapers and dark stools on day 3
Relative who needed phototherapy
Cesarean birth for breech
Hepatitis B vaccine given
Apgars 8 and 9

items.q: Complete the nurse's analysis.
items.rationale: Early jaundice suggests hemolysis or another pathologic process. Treatment thresholds depend on age in hours, gestational age and risk factors. Output targets rise each day (by day 3-4, at least 4-6 wet diapers and transitional stools), and weight loss above about 7-8% warrants a feeding assessment and plan.
items.text: Jaundice that appears in the first {0} of life is always considered pathologic. This baby's bilirubin of 17.8 mg/dL at 68 hours is {1} his phototherapy threshold of about 16 mg/dL. By day 3, a well-fed baby usually has at least {2}. A weight loss of {3} suggests feeding is not adequate and needs evaluation.

options: 24 hours
5 days
above
below
3-4 wet diapers and stools turning green-yellow
1 wet diaper and black stools
more than 7-8%

items.q: Classify each phototherapy practice as correct or incorrect.
items.rationale: Effective phototherapy needs maximum skin exposure and eye protection. Lotions can cause burns and reduce effectiveness. Interruptions are kept short (feeds of up to about 30 minutes) during intensive phototherapy. Phototherapy increases insensible water loss and can affect temperature. Light can degrade bilirubin in the sample, and skin color is unreliable once phototherapy starts, so serum levels are used.
rows: Cover the eyes with opaque shields and check under them regularly
Apply a moisturizing lotion to prevent dry skin
Stop phototherapy for 2 hours at every feed so he can be held
Monitor temperature, hydration and number of wet diapers
Turn off the lights when drawing blood for bilirubin
Rely on skin color to judge whether bilirubin is falling

items.q: Chioma cries, "I have no milk. Just give him formula." What is the nurse's best response?
items.rationale: This response acknowledges her pain and fear, gives accurate information (her milk is coming in), offers practical help, and respects her decision while protecting her breastfeeding goal. Medical supplementation is indicated here because of jaundice and weight loss; how it is given (after the breast, with expressed milk first) supports milk supply. Shaming her, dismissing her concerns, or giving up without exploring her goals are not supportive.
options: "Breast is best; you have to keep trying without formula."
"Formula is fine; I'll bring a bottle and you can rest."

"You're in a lot of pain and worried about him. Your breasts are filling, and we can help with the latch and pain. Would you like to work on it together, and use your expressed milk (or formula if needed) after feeds while your milk comes in?"
"It's normal to have no milk on day 3. Don't worry."

items.q: Which breastfeeding interventions are appropriate now? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: A deeper latch reduces nipple trauma; the football hold suits a cesarean. Frequent feeds, breast compression and expressing protect supply and increase intake. Water or glucose water does not lower bilirubin, reduces milk intake and can cause hyponatremia. Partner involvement and lactation expertise increase success.
options: Help with a deep, asymmetric latch and try a football hold, which avoids pressure on her incision
Feed at least 8-12 times in 24 hours, waking him if needed
Teach breast compression during the feed to keep a sleepy baby swallowing
Hand express or pump after feeds and give the expressed milk
Give water or glucose water between feeds to help clear the bilirubin
Arrange the lactation consultant visit and involve Emeka in positioning and pump care
Apply expressed breast milk to nipples and assess for proper latch to heal cracks

items.q: Put the nurse's priorities for this morning in order.
items.rationale: Effective phototherapy and infant stability come first to bring the bilirubin down. Adequate intake is part of treatment. Addressing the mother's pain enables feeding. The repeat level is drawn at the ordered time, and teaching follows once immediate needs are met.
options: Feed now with latch support and supplementation as ordered
Treat Chioma's nipple pain and arrange the lactation consult
Teach the parents about jaundice, phototherapy and feeding goals at home
Confirm phototherapy is working correctly (irradiance, skin exposure, eye shields) and the baby is stable
Obtain the repeat bilirubin at the ordered time

items.q: Write discharge teaching for Chioma and Emeka about jaundice once phototherapy is complete. Include feeding targets and the signs that should make them seek care urgently.
items.rationale: Credit specific feeding and output targets, follow-up, and urgent warning signs (including signs of bilirubin encephalopathy and pale stools), in reassuring language.
items.model: Feeding: breastfeed 8-12 times in 24 hours; wake him if he sleeps more than 3 hours; look for swallowing; at least 6 wet diapers and 3-4 yellow, seedy stools a day by day 5-7; keep the follow-up appointment (often within 1-2 days) for a weight and bilirubin check. Jaundice: some yellow color may return (rebound), so check his skin and eyes in daylight. Seek care urgently for: yellow color spreading to the legs or getting deeper, very sleepy or hard to wake, not feeding, fewer wet diapers, pale or white stools or dark urine, high-pitched cry, arching or stiffness, fever. Emphasize that jaundice is common and treatable, and that they did nothing wrong.

cases.title: Case 25: Asking the Hard Question: Suicide Risk After an Intentional Overdose
cases.short: Asking the Hard Question: Suicide Risk After an Intentional Overdose
cases.group: Unit 5 · Mental health, safety and ethics
cases.description: A 22-year-old student is in the emergency department after an intentional acetaminophen overdose. Treat the medical emergency, assess suicide risk directly and compassionately, and keep her safe.
objectives: Ask about suicide directly and use a structured screen.
Distinguish risk factors, warning signs and protective factors.
Implement environmental safety and observation for a patient at high risk.
Recognize the time-critical treatment of acetaminophen overdose.
cases.scenario: You are the emergency department nurse. Sara Lindqvist was brought in by her roommate at 21:30. She told triage she "took a bunch of pills to sleep and not wake up."

items.q: When you begin your assessment, how should you ask Sara about suicide?
items.rationale: Asking directly and non-judgmentally, using the words "killing yourself", is recommended and does not increase risk. Leading questions invite a "no" answer, "why" questions feel judgmental, and avoiding the topic leaves risk unassessed.
options: "You're not thinking of hurting yourself again, are you?"
"Why would you want to do something like this?"
"Sometimes when people feel this hopeless, they think about killing themselves. Are you thinking about killing yourself now?"
Avoid the topic until psychiatry arrives, to avoid putting the idea in her head

items.q: Classify each finding as a risk factor or warning sign, or as a protective factor.
items.rationale: Giving away possessions, recent losses, family history of suicide, untreated depression and persistent wishes to be dead increase risk. Connectedness (her roommate) and reasons for living (her dog, her family) are protective factors that can be built into a safety plan, though they do not reduce the need for close observation now.
rows: Gave her roommate a favorite jacket yesterday
Recent breakup and loss of her scholarship
A close roommate who found her and brought her in
Stopped her antidepressant and therapy a year ago
Says she loves her dog at her parents' house

items.q: Which safety measures are required while Sara is in the emergency department? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: High-risk patients need constant observation, a safe environment and searches of items that enter the room, explained respectfully. No-harm contracts are not effective and do not replace assessment. A patient at high risk must not be left alone; if she tries to leave before evaluation, the emergency hold process applies.
options: Continuous 1:1 observation within arm's length, including in the bathroom
Remove belongings, cords, drawstrings, sharps and anything that could be used for self-harm
Check the room for ligature points and hazardous equipment
Allow her to leave if she promises not to hurt herself (a no-harm contract)
Explain the reasons for the measures to her in a calm, respectful way
Check meal trays and items brought by visitors
Leave her alone to rest so she does not feel watched

items.q: Complete the reasoning about her acetaminophen overdose.
items.rationale: 10,000 mg ÷ 60 kg ≈ 167 mg/kg, a potentially toxic dose (above about 150 mg/kg). The level is plotted on the Rumack-Matthew nomogram from 4 hours after ingestion. Acetylcysteine replenishes glutathione and is most effective within 8 hours. Early in poisoning, liver tests are often normal; injury develops over the following days.
items.text: Sara took about {0} of acetaminophen. Her 6-hour level of 160 mcg/mL is {1} the treatment line, so she needs acetylcysteine, which works best when started within {2} of ingestion. Her normal liver tests now {3}.

options: 167 mg/kg
16 mg/kg
above
below
8 hours
48 hours
mean she will not be harmed
do not rule out liver injury, which usually peaks 2-4 days after ingestion

items.q: Put the nurse's priorities in order on arrival.
items.rationale: Immediate safety from self-harm and time-critical antidote treatment come first and happen together. A structured risk assessment and rapport-building follow; family involvement is discussed with her consent, within the limits of confidentiality when there is a risk to life.
options: Ensure continuous 1:1 observation and a safe environment
Complete the suicide risk screen and mental status assessment
Start the acetylcysteine as ordered (time-critical)
Build rapport: listen to her story and her losses
Talk with her about contacting her mother and about her consent

items.q: Sara says, "Please don't write down what I told you. And I want to go home now." What is the best response?
items.rationale: Confidentiality has limits when there is a risk to life; the nurse is honest about this while staying empathic and explaining the plan. Promising secrecy or discharge is unsafe, and threats damage trust (holds and security are used only if needed, following policy and law).
options: "Okay, I won't write it down."
"You can go home once the IV finishes."

"I can hear that you want to go home. What you told me is important for keeping you safe, so I need to share it with the team. I want to help you get through this; you will need to stay while we treat the overdose and the psychiatrist talks with you."
"If you try to leave, security will restrain you."

items.q: Before she is transferred, describe the elements of a safety plan you would begin with Sara (to be completed with her mental health team), using details from her chart.
items.rationale: Credit a structured plan with her own warning signs, coping strategies, people, professional and crisis contacts, means restriction and reasons for living. A plan supports, but does not replace, ongoing professional care.
items.model: Safety plan elements (Stanley-Brown): 1. Her warning signs (withdrawing, sleeping all day, not eating, giving things away, thoughts that "it would be better"). 2. Internal coping strategies (things she can do alone: walking, music, a shower). 3. People and places for distraction (her roommate Maya, a café on campus). 4. People she can ask for help (roommate, mother when she is ready, a trusted friend). 5. Professionals and crisis lines (campus counseling, her future therapist, 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline in the US or the local emergency number). 6. Making the environment safe (no stockpiles of medicines: roommate holds medicines, small pack sizes; confirm no firearms). Also: reasons for living (her dog, finishing her degree differently), restart treatment for depression, plan for academic support (scholarship appeal, student services).

cases.title: Case 26: Narrow Margin: Lithium Toxicity in Bipolar Disorder
cases.short: Narrow Margin: Lithium Toxicity in Bipolar Disorder
cases.group: Unit 5 · Mental health, safety and ethics
cases.description: A 49-year-old man stable on lithium for years develops vomiting, coarse tremor and confusion after a new diuretic, an NSAID and a stomach bug. Recognize toxicity, act, and teach to prevent it.
objectives: Recognize signs of lithium toxicity by level and severity.
Identify drug interactions and fluid states that raise lithium levels.
Take the correct actions for suspected toxicity.
Teach safe lithium use.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the medical unit. Thomas Reid was admitted from the emergency department at 06:00 with vomiting and confusion.

items.q: Highlight the findings that indicate lithium toxicity rather than expected side effects.
items.rationale: A fine tremor, mild thirst and hypothyroidism are common with therapeutic lithium. Coarse tremor, ataxia, dysarthria, confusion, neuromuscular irritability, persistent GI symptoms and a level above 1.5 mEq/L indicate toxicity; above 2.0 is moderate to severe.
options: Coarse tremor (cannot hold a cup)
Slurred speech and unsteady gait
Confusion about the date
Muscle fasciculations and hyperreflexia
Lithium level 2.4 mEq/L
Hypothyroidism on levothyroxine
Mild thirst (on his usual dose)
Persistent vomiting and diarrhea

items.q: For each factor, decide whether it raises lithium levels.
items.rationale: Lithium is handled like sodium by the kidneys. Thiazides, NSAIDs, ACE inhibitors and ARBs, dehydration, low sodium intake and kidney injury increase reabsorption or reduce excretion, raising levels. Levothyroxine does not interact, and steady fluid and salt intake keeps levels stable.
rows: Vomiting and diarrhea (volume and sodium loss)
Drinking 2-3 L of fluid a day with a normal salt intake

items.q: At 08:45, which action should the nurse take regarding the 09:00 medications?
items.rationale: The admission orders reconciled his home medicines without accounting for the toxicity. Lithium must be held with a level of 2.4, and the interacting drugs (thiazide, NSAID) stopped; the nurse questions the orders with the provider. Partial doses still add to toxicity.
options: Give the lithium on time because missing doses can cause relapse
Hold the lithium, hydrochlorothiazide and ibuprofen and contact the provider to discontinue them
Give half the lithium dose
Give all medications and recheck the level in 6 hours

items.q: Complete the bow-tie for Thomas.
items.rationale: The neurological signs and the level indicate lithium toxicity worsened by kidney injury. Treatment is to stop lithium and interacting drugs and restore volume with isotonic saline to improve excretion (dialysis if severe). Loop diuretics and fluid restriction worsen sodium loss and toxicity. Serial levels, renal function and neuro status show progress; lithium can redistribute from tissues, so levels may rebound.
conditions: Lithium toxicity with acute kidney injury
actions: Hold lithium and interacting drugs, and notify the provider
Continue isotonic IV fluids as ordered and keep strict intake and output
Give furosemide to increase lithium excretion
Restrict fluids to 1 L/day
Give an extra dose of levothyroxine
monitors: Neurological status (confusion, tremor, gait) and seizure activity

items.q: Complete the nurse's explanation of lithium levels.
items.rationale: Lithium has a narrow therapeutic index. Trough levels (12 hours post-dose) are used. Hemodialysis removes lithium efficiently and is considered for very high levels, severe neurological toxicity or impaired kidney function.
items.text: For maintenance, the usual therapeutic lithium range is about {0}, and levels are drawn {1}. A level above {2} mEq/L suggests toxicity. Because Thomas has severe neurological signs and kidney impairment with a level above 2.5 if it rises, the team may consider {3}.

options: 12 hours after the last dose
1 hour after a dose
hemodialysis
a higher lithium dose
