items.q: Thomas is recovering. Write teaching for Thomas and Amy to prevent lithium toxicity in the future, including what to do during an illness like this one.
items.rationale: Credit steady fluids and salt, a sick-day plan (contact prescriber, possible temporary hold), interaction avoidance (NSAIDs, thiazides, ACE inhibitors and ARBs), toxicity signs and routine monitoring.
items.model: Keep fluid (about 2-3 L/day) and salt intake steady; do not start a low-salt diet without discussing it. During illness with vomiting, diarrhea, fever or poor intake, or in heat or heavy sweating: call the prescriber the same day; he may be told to hold lithium temporarily and get a level, rather than continuing as usual. Avoid NSAIDs (ibuprofen, naproxen); use acetaminophen. Tell every prescriber and pharmacist he takes lithium, especially before starting diuretics, ACE inhibitors or ARBs for blood pressure. Know early toxicity signs (worsening tremor, nausea, diarrhea, unsteadiness, slurred speech, confusion) and seek urgent care for them. Keep regular lithium, kidney and thyroid tests. Amy can help watch for signs and should know the plan.

cases.title: Case 27: Person-Centered Dementia Care: Agitation Without Restraints
cases.short: Person-Centered Dementia Care: Agitation Without Restraints
cases.group: Unit 5 · Mental health, safety and ethics
cases.description: An 86-year-old man with Alzheimer's disease and a urinary tract infection becomes agitated every evening, tries to leave "to go to work," and strikes out during care. His son asks for restraints. Find the unmet needs and create a person-centered plan.
objectives: Distinguish delirium from dementia and recognize delirium superimposed on dementia.
Identify unmet needs (pain, constipation, fear, routine) behind behavioral symptoms.
Choose non-pharmacological, least restrictive interventions.
Create and evaluate a person-centered care plan with the family.
cases.scenario: You are the evening nurse on the medical unit. It is 17:30 and Arthur Bennett is standing at the unit doors, shouting, "Let me out, I'll be late for the 6 o'clock train!"

items.q: Highlight the unmet needs and triggers that may be driving Arthur's behavior.
items.rationale: Behavior in dementia often communicates an unmet need: pain, constipation, dehydration, sensory loss, fear when touched without explanation, and routines from his working life. Benzodiazepines worsen delirium in older adults. The haloperidol allergy is important for safety but is not a trigger.
options: PAINAD 6 with hip guarding; his home scheduled acetaminophen was not continued
No bowel movement for 3 days with a firm abdomen
Glasses and hearing aids not in place (dead batteries)
Brief changed without warning by a hurried staff member
Late afternoon is when he used to leave for the 6 o'clock train
Sodium 146 and dry mouth, drinks little water
Lorazepam given last night, after which he was more confused
Allergy to haloperidol

items.q: Classify each feature as more typical of delirium or of dementia.
items.rationale: Delirium is acute, fluctuating, marked by inattention and usually caused by a medical problem; it is a medical emergency. Dementia is gradual and progressive. People with dementia are at high risk of delirium, as here (CAM positive with a UTI).
rows: Acute onset over hours to days
Often reversible when the cause (such as infection) is treated
New change from his baseline noticed by his son on admission

items.q: Arthur is at the doors shouting that he will be late for the 6 o'clock train. What is the best response?
items.rationale: Validating the feeling behind the statement (his pride in being punctual), entering his reality briefly and redirecting with something meaningful (tea, as he likes it) reduces distress. Reorienting by arguing increases agitation, and threats or guilt escalate the situation.
options: "Mr. Bennett, there is no train. You retired 20 years ago and you are in the hospital."
"Mr. Bennett, you've always been on time for your trains. Come and sit with me while we check the timetable, and have a cup of tea with milk and two sugars."
"If you don't go back to your room, I'll call security."
"Your son will be very upset if you leave."

items.q: Which interventions belong in a person-centered plan for Arthur? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Treating pain and constipation, supporting hydration and senses, gentle communication, meaningful activities and family presence at the predictable time address the causes. Restraints increase agitation, injury and delirium and are a last resort; scheduled benzodiazepines worsen delirium and fall risk.
options: Restart scheduled acetaminophen and reassess pain with PAINAD
Start a bowel regimen and offer fluids he likes (tea) regularly
Replace hearing aid batteries and put on his glasses
Explain each step of care before touching him, approaching from the front
Play brass band music and read him the newspaper in the late afternoon
Apply wrist restraints at night so he does not wander
Give lorazepam at 16:00 every day before he becomes agitated
Ask his son to visit at the time agitation usually starts, and keep the evening bath routine

items.q: Complete the nurse's reasoning about pain.
items.rationale: PAINAD is validated for people with advanced dementia: 1-3 mild, 4-6 moderate, 7-10 severe. Pain is under-recognized and under-treated in dementia and often appears as behavior change.
items.text: Arthur cannot rate his pain on a 0-10 scale, so the nurse uses the {0} scale, which rates breathing, vocalization, facial expression, body language and consolability. His score of 6 out of 10 indicates {1} pain. Untreated pain in people with dementia commonly shows up as {2}.

options: PAINAD
Glasgow Coma
mild
moderate to severe
agitation, resistance to care and striking out
improved appetite

items.q: Peter, Arthur's son, says, "Please tie him down tonight or give him something to knock him out." What should the nurse say?
items.rationale: The nurse acknowledges the son's concern, explains the risks of restraints and sedatives (and Arthur's haloperidol reaction), shares the assessment and partners with the family on alternatives. A family request does not justify restraints, which require an individual assessment and a provider order as a last resort.
options: "I'll call the doctor for a haloperidol order."
"Yes, we can apply restraints if the family asks."

"I can see how worried you are about his safety. Restraints and strong sedatives can make his confusion worse and cause falls and injuries. We think pain, constipation and missing his hearing aids are part of the problem. Can we go through what usually calms him, and could you stay with him this evening?"
"There's nothing more we can do."

items.q: Create a person-centered evening plan (16:00-22:00) for Arthur, using his life story and preferences, and describe how you will evaluate whether it works over the next two evenings.
items.rationale: Credit a timed plan that pre-empts the predictable agitation, uses his history and preferences, addresses pain, hydration, elimination and senses, involves family, avoids restraints and benzodiazepines, and has measurable evaluation criteria.
items.model: Plan: 15:30 give scheduled acetaminophen (ordered) so pain is controlled before the usual agitation; check hearing aids and glasses are on. 16:00 tea with milk and two sugars and a biscuit; offer fluids every hour; toileting before he becomes restless. 16:30-17:30 meaningful activity linked to his railway career (a railway book or photos, a "timetable" to look at, talking about trains), brass band music; walk with him (safe supervised mobility) rather than stopping him. 18:00 son visits for dinner and stays through the evening. 19:30 warm wash or bath as at home; explain each step, approach from the front, one person, unhurried. 21:00 donepezil; quiet, dim lights, same caregiver if possible; in bed by 21:30. Bowel regimen. Avoid lorazepam; no restraints. Evaluate: number and intensity of agitation episodes (from a behavior log), PAINAD scores, CAM, sleep hours, intake and bowel movements, need for PRN medications, falls or injuries, staff and family feedback; adjust the plan with the team and Peter.

cases.title: Case 28: Honoring Her Wishes: Goals of Care at the End of Life
cases.short: Honoring Her Wishes: Goals of Care at the End of Life
cases.group: Unit 5 · Mental health, safety and ethics
cases.description: A 77-year-old woman with metastatic pancreatic cancer is dying. Her advance directive declines life support, her daughter is her health care proxy, and her son wants "everything done." Recognize the dying process, manage symptoms, and support an ethical family conversation.
objectives: Recognize the signs of approaching death.
Provide comfort-focused symptom management.
Apply ethical principles and the role of the health care proxy.
Communicate with a family in conflict and respect cultural and religious practices.
cases.scenario: You are the night nurse on the oncology unit. Miriam Feldman's family is gathered. At 22:00 her son Daniel stops you: "Why is nobody doing anything? She needs to go to intensive care."

items.q: Highlight the signs that Miriam is likely in the last hours to days of life.
items.rationale: Altered breathing patterns, terminal secretions, mottling, decreased urine output, reduced consciousness and falling blood pressure are common signs of imminent death. Recognizing them lets the nurse prepare the family and focus on comfort.
options: Cheyne-Stokes breathing with pauses of 15-20 seconds
Noisy, gurgling respirations ("death rattle")
Mottling and coolness of the knees and feet
Urine 60 mL in 8 hours
Mostly unresponsive, opening eyes briefly to her name
Morphine allergy (nausea)
Weak radial pulse with BP 84/50

items.q: Daniel says, "Why is nobody doing anything? She needs to go to intensive care." What is the nurse's best initial response?
items.rationale: Daniel's request comes from shock and grief. Acknowledging his feelings and inviting him to talk opens the door to explaining her prognosis and her own wishes, and to arranging a family meeting. Pointing to legal authority first, offering treatment she refused, or saying "nothing more can be done" (when comfort care is active care) is not therapeutic.
options: "Your sister is the proxy, so it is her decision, not yours."
"You've just arrived and this must be a shock to see her like this. Would you sit down with me and tell me what you are seeing and what worries you most?"
"We can transfer her to the ICU if you want."
"There's nothing more we can do for her."

items.q: Complete the explanation of decision-making.
items.rationale: A designated proxy makes decisions based on the patient's known wishes (substituted judgment) or, if unknown, her best interests. Honoring her advance directive respects autonomy; relieving suffering and avoiding burdensome interventions reflect beneficence and non-maleficence.
items.text: Because Miriam can no longer speak for herself, decisions are made by her health care proxy, {0}. The proxy should use {1}, guided by her advance directive and what she said at the family meeting. Respecting her refusal of life support honors the ethical principle of {2}, and focusing on comfort reflects {3}.

options: Daniel
Rachel
their own preferences
substituted judgment: what Miriam would want
justice
autonomy
beneficence and non-maleficence
veracity

items.q: For each intervention, decide whether it fits Miriam's comfort-focused plan.
items.rationale: Anticholinergics and positioning reduce terminal secretions; deep suctioning is distressing and usually ineffective. Mouth care relieves dryness. Opioids relieve pain and dyspnea at the end of life. Feeding tubes, routine vital signs and labs do not add comfort and were declined. Hearing is thought to persist late, so families are encouraged to talk to the patient.
rows: Give glycopyrrolate for the noisy secretions and reposition her on her side
Mouth care with moist swabs and lip balm every 1-2 hours
Morphine bolus for grimacing or labored breathing
Check vital signs every hour and draw morning labs
Invite the family to hold her hand and talk to her; hearing may remain

items.q: Daniel asks, "Is the morphine killing her? Her breathing is so strange." Which statement by the nurse is accurate?
items.rationale: Appropriately titrated opioids for pain and dyspnea at the end of life do not hasten death (the principle of double effect also supports intent to relieve suffering). Cheyne-Stokes breathing is part of the dying process. Stopping comfort medication would cause suffering.
options: "Yes, the morphine is speeding things up, but it's what she wanted."
"Her breathing pattern is part of the natural dying process. The morphine is given in doses to relieve her pain and breathlessness, and used this way it does not shorten life."
"We will stop the morphine so you can see whether she improves."
"Morphine is a sedative that keeps her asleep."

items.q: Which actions respect the family's religious and cultural wishes? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: In Jewish tradition, burial often takes place quickly, the body may be watched and is prepared by a burial society, and families may have specific wishes about care after death. The nurse supports these by involving spiritual care, asking rather than assuming, and coordinating timely paperwork. Practices vary between families, so asking is essential.
options: Call the family's rabbi or the hospital chaplain now, as the family requested
Ask the family which practices are important to them before and after death, rather than assuming
Allow family members to stay with her continuously, including after death (some families arrange for someone to stay with the body)
Contact the bereavement coordinator and the provider so that death paperwork can be completed promptly for a quick burial
Routinely wash and prepare the body before the family is asked
Ask before removing lines and tubes after death and whether the family wants a Jewish burial society (Chevra Kadisha) involved

items.q: Plan the family meeting you would request for the morning with Rachel, Daniel, the palliative care team and the rabbi. List who should attend and write how you would open the meeting and explain Miriam's condition and wishes in plain language.
items.rationale: Credit appropriate attendees, an opening that asks for each person's understanding, a plain-language explanation of dying and of Miriam's own wishes, empathic attention to Daniel, and a shared plan including religious needs.
items.model: Attendees: Rachel (proxy), Daniel, the attending or palliative care physician, the nurse caring for Miriam, social worker or chaplain and the family's rabbi if they wish; a quiet private room with time set aside. Opening: introductions; "We're here to talk about how your mother is doing and how we can best care for her. First, can you each tell us what you understand about her illness?" Then explain (physician leads, nurse supports): "Your mother's cancer has spread and is now causing her body to shut down. The changes in her breathing, her cool, mottled skin and how little she is passing urine tell us she is likely to die within hours to a few days. Two weeks ago she told us and Rachel: 'I'm ready, no machines, I want to be comfortable with my family.' Her written directive says the same. Intensive care, a breathing machine or a feeding tube could not reverse the cancer and would not give her the peace she asked for." Ask Daniel what he needs; acknowledge his grief and the difficulty of arriving late; invite him to spend time with her; reassure the family about comfort medicines; discuss rituals and what will happen at the time of death; agree on the plan together.

cases.title: Case 29: Behind Closed Doors: Recognizing Intimate Partner Violence in Pregnancy
cases.short: Behind Closed Doors: Recognizing Intimate Partner Violence in Pregnancy
cases.group: Unit 5 · Mental health, safety and ethics
cases.description: At a 24-week prenatal visit, a 27-year-old woman has bruises at different stages of healing, a partner who answers for her, missed appointments and a positive depression screen. Create a private space, ask, document and plan for safety.
objectives: Recognize cues of intimate partner violence (IPV) in pregnancy.
Screen privately and respond without judgment.
Document injuries objectively and understand reporting obligations.
Support autonomy and plan for safety with the patient.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse in a prenatal clinic. Natalie Brooks is here for her 24-week visit with her partner, Jason.

items.q: Highlight the cues that suggest intimate partner violence.
items.rationale: Controlling behavior, patterned bruises of different ages, injuries inconsistent with the explanation, missed care, depression, poor weight gain and restarting smoking are associated with IPV, which often begins or escalates in pregnancy. The fetal heart rate and blood type are normal findings.
options: Partner answers for her and wants to stay for the whole visit
Fingertip-pattern bruises at different stages of healing
Explanation ("I bump into things") that does not match the injury
Missed prenatal visits
Depression screen score of 14
Poor weight gain and fundal height smaller than expected
Fetal heart rate 148/min
Blood type B positive

items.q: How should the nurse create an opportunity to talk with Natalie alone?
items.rationale: Using a universal, routine policy to separate the patient from a partner is safe and non-accusatory. Confronting the partner or asking in front of him can increase danger. Waiting may miss the only chance to help.
options: "Jason, I think you're hurting her. Please leave the room."
"Jason, as part of our routine for every patient, I see each person on their own for part of the visit. You and Lily can wait in the family room; I'll come and get you."
Ask Natalie in front of Jason whether she feels safe at home
Wait until the next visit to see whether she comes alone

items.q: Alone with Natalie, which question is best?
items.rationale: Normalizing the question, asking about specific behaviors and gently naming what was observed makes disclosure easier. Labels such as "victim", "why do you stay" and statements about the partner can feel judgmental and close the conversation.
options: "Are you a victim of domestic violence?"
"Why do you stay with someone who hurts you?"
"Because violence is common in many women's lives, I ask everyone: has anyone hit, kicked, choked or hurt you, or made you feel afraid? I noticed the bruises on your arm."
"Jason seems controlling. Is he?"

items.q: Natalie discloses that Jason grabs and pushes her when he is angry, and it has been worse since she became pregnant. Which nursing actions are appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Validation, objective documentation, danger assessment, safe resources, transparency about reporting laws and attention to the child's safety are core. Pressuring her to leave removes her control; leaving is often the most dangerous time, and she is the expert on her own safety. Reporting rules for adult IPV vary by jurisdiction, while suspected child abuse must be reported.
options: Thank her for telling you and say that it is not her fault
Document her statements in quotation marks and the bruises objectively (size, color, location, body map, photographs with consent)
Assess immediate danger (for example, choking or strangulation, threats to kill, a weapon in the home, escalation in pregnancy)
Tell her she must leave Jason today for the baby's sake
Give information about the national or local domestic violence hotline and advocacy services in a safe way (for example a number written on something discreet)
Explain any reporting your state or country requires and what will happen, before she shares more if possible
Ask whether her daughter has been harmed or has witnessed violence

items.q: Classify each statement about documentation as appropriate or inappropriate.
items.rationale: Documentation should quote the patient, describe injuries objectively, and record resources offered and her choices. Conclusions ("victim") and words that suggest doubt ("claims") are inappropriate. Careful records can support the patient later.
rows: "Patient states, 'He grabbed my arm and pushed me into the wall on Saturday.'"
"Patient is a victim of abuse by her boyfriend."
"Four oval bruises, 1-1.5 cm, left upper arm, purple and yellow-green (see body map)."
"Hotline information provided; patient declined a printed brochure because partner checks her bag."

items.q: Complete the nurse's reasoning.
items.rationale: Pregnancy is a time of increased risk. IPV is linked to poor fetal growth, preterm birth, depression and substance use. Non-fatal strangulation sharply increases the risk of homicide. Respecting her autonomy, while offering support and safety planning, is central.
items.text: Intimate partner violence often {0} during pregnancy. It is associated with {1}. A history of {2} is a major predictor of future lethal violence and should always be asked about. The decision about leaving belongs to {3}.

options: begins or escalates
stops
preterm birth, low birth weight and maternal depression
gestational diabetes only
strangulation or choking
arguments
the nurse
Natalie

items.q: Natalie says she is not ready to leave, but she wants to be safer. Describe the elements of a safety plan you would begin with her today and how you will arrange follow-up that does not alert Jason.
items.rationale: Credit practical, patient-led safety measures, safe resources, attention to her daughter, and a follow-up plan that protects her privacy, plus referrals for depression and fetal growth concerns.
items.model: Safety plan: identify a safe person she can call and a code word; plan where she could go in an emergency (a friend, a shelter) and how (keep a charged phone, some money and keys); keep important documents (IDs, birth certificates, insurance, medicines, prenatal records) in a safe place or with a trusted person; learn the hotline and local advocacy services; teach her daughter how to call emergency services if old enough; identify warning signs that violence is escalating and the safest rooms (avoid the kitchen and rooms with weapons); call emergency services if in immediate danger. Follow-up: agree on a safe phone number and time to call, or link follow-up to routine prenatal visits (for example, adding an extra "routine" visit for the glucose test or growth scan); connect her with an on-site advocate or social worker today if she agrees; address depression and smoking with referrals; respect her choices and leave the door open.

cases.title: Case 30: Can He Afford to Recover? Medication Costs After a Heart Attack
cases.short: Can He Afford to Recover? Medication Costs After a Heart Attack
cases.description: A 56-year-old rideshare driver with a high-deductible plan is going home after a stent with six new prescriptions. Estimate his monthly costs from the chart, find resources, decide which medicine he must never stop, and plan for adherence.
objectives: Collect financial and social data from the chart to prepare discharge counseling.
Estimate a patient's monthly out-of-pocket medication costs.
Identify resources to make medicines affordable and the team members who can help.
Plan teaching that protects the most critical medication and reinforces adherence.
cases.scenario: You are the discharge nurse on the cardiac step-down unit. Rafael Gomez is going home this afternoon after a drug-eluting stent. As you start teaching, he says quietly: "I don't know how I'm going to pay for all of this."

items.q: Highlight the findings that put Rafael at risk of cost-related medication non-adherence.
items.rationale: Deductible exposure, unstable income, an expensive brand medicine, a past pattern of stopping medicines, and his own expressed worries are strong predictors of cost-related non-adherence. EF and potassium are clinical findings; his smartphone is a resource (reminders, discount apps).
options: High-deductible plan with $2,950 of the deductible still to meet
Self-employed with variable income; worried about missing work
Ticagrelor is brand-only at $430 for 30 days before his deductible is met
Stopped a blood pressure pill years ago when it ran out
Asked whether the pills are expensive and how many rehab sessions he must pay for
Ejection fraction 50%
Uses a smartphone
Potassium 4.4 mEq/L

items.q: Use the price table to estimate Rafael's first-month cost with his plan (before the deductible is met).
items.rationale: 4 + 430 + 15 + 10 + 5 = $464; + $20 = $484. 430 ÷ 484 ≈ 89%. With the copay card ($10): 4 + 10 + 15 + 10 + 5 = $44. Estimating costs makes the problem concrete and guides which resources to pursue.
items.text: With his plan, the five daily medicines cost: aspirin $4 + ticagrelor $430 + atorvastatin $15 + metoprolol $10 + lisinopril $5 = {0} per month, plus nitroglycerin $20 the first month for a total of {1}. Ticagrelor makes up about {2} of the monthly cost. If the ticagrelor copay card applies, the five daily medicines would cost about {3} per month.

items.q: Rafael says, "If money is tight, which pill can I skip?" Which medicine is the most dangerous for him to stop?
items.rationale: Stopping dual antiplatelet therapy early after a drug-eluting stent can cause stent thrombosis, a sudden, often fatal heart attack. All of his medicines matter, so the nurse does not suggest skipping any, but ticagrelor and aspirin must never be stopped without cardiology. If cost is a barrier, the prescriber can consider an affordable alternative (for example generic clopidogrel) rather than the patient stopping.
options: Atorvastatin
Metoprolol succinate
Ticagrelor (with aspirin)
Lisinopril

items.q: For each resource, decide whether it is an appropriate step for Rafael's team to take.
items.rationale: Copay cards, assistance programs, prescriber review of therapeutic alternatives, discount programs, social work and meds-to-beds services reduce cost and gaps. Changing doses on his own is unsafe, and unverified websites risk counterfeit medicines.
rows: Ask the pharmacist to run the ticagrelor manufacturer copay card and check the patient assistance program
Ask the prescriber whether a lower-cost generic antiplatelet (such as clopidogrel) is clinically appropriate
Suggest Rafael take ticagrelor once a day instead of twice to make it last
Use a pharmacy generic discount list or discount app for the generic medicines
Refer to social work for financial counseling, hospital charity care and a plan review at open enrollment
Fill the prescriptions through meds-to-beds so he leaves with medicine in hand
Tell him to buy the medicines from an unverified overseas website

items.q: Put the nurse's discharge actions in order.
items.rationale: Assess first, then mobilize resources while he is still in hospital, and involve the prescriber if therapy must change. Teaching is most useful once the final, affordable regimen is known. He should leave with medicines in hand and realistic follow-up.
options: Confirm he leaves with a 30-day supply and the follow-up and rehab appointments he can attend
Contact pharmacy (meds-to-beds) and social work to apply cost resources before he leaves
Acknowledge his worry and ask what he can afford and which costs concern him most
Teach each medicine's purpose, especially why ticagrelor and aspirin must never be stopped, using teach-back
Communicate with the prescriber about any cost barrier that requires a change in therapy

items.q: Which strategies would reinforce Rafael's long-term adherence? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Reminders, organizers, longer supplies, family involvement, a plan for cost changes, linking savings from quitting smoking, and supported rehabilitation improve adherence. Feeling well is the goal of treatment, not a reason to stop.
options: Set phone alarms for the twice-daily ticagrelor and use a weekly pill organizer
Ask about 90-day supplies and automatic refills once costs are settled
Involve his wife and link doses to routines (breakfast and dinner)
Tell him to call the cardiology clinic or pharmacist before he runs out or if a cost changes, rather than stopping
Advise him to stop the medicines once he feels well
Discuss how quitting smoking also saves money he can put toward medicines
Explain cardiac rehabilitation benefits and ask social work about coverage options

items.q: Write what you would say to Rafael to explain why ticagrelor is so important, and three teach-back questions to confirm he understands his medicine plan and what to do if he cannot afford a refill.
items.rationale: Credit a plain-language explanation of stent thrombosis and teach-back questions about the critical drugs, a cost plan that avoids stopping, and chest pain response.
items.model: Explanation: "The stent the doctor put in your heart artery is like a small metal tube. For the next year, your blood can form a clot inside it, which would cause another heart attack. Ticagrelor and aspirin together keep that from happening. That's why these two are the most important pills: take ticagrelor twice a day, every day, and never stop them unless your heart doctor tells you to, even if you feel fine." Teach-back: 1. "Tell me which two pills protect your stent and when you take them." 2. "What will you do if you are getting low on ticagrelor and the price is a problem?" (Answer: call the pharmacy, clinic or social worker before running out; do not skip or stretch doses.) 3. "What will you do if you get chest pain?" (Nitroglycerin 1 tablet under the tongue; call emergency services if not better after 5 minutes.) Also acceptable: "Which number will you call about the copay card?"

cases.title: Case 31: Speaking Up: Early Warning Scores, SBAR and the Chain of Command
cases.short: Speaking Up: Early Warning Scores, SBAR and the Chain of Command
cases.description: A 70-year-old man with pneumonia is deteriorating at 02:00. Calculate his NEWS2 score, write an SBAR, and know what to do when the on-call physician says to "keep an eye on him."
objectives: Calculate and interpret an early warning score (NEWS2).
Write an effective SBAR with a clear recommendation.
Use closed-loop communication and read-back.
Escalate through the chain of command when concerns are not addressed.
cases.scenario: You are the night nurse on the medical unit. At 02:00 you check on Walter Brooks, admitted yesterday with pneumonia.

items.q: Use the NEWS2 chart in Documents to score Walter at 02:00.
items.rationale: 3 + 3 + 2 + 2 + 2 + 3 + 1 = 16. A NEWS2 of 7 or more is high risk and requires an emergency response; the 22:00 score was 0 + 1 + 2 + 0 + 1 + 0 + 0 = 4. The rapid rise and new confusion are particularly concerning (possible sepsis and respiratory failure).
items.text: Respiratory rate 26 scores {0}; SpO₂ 91% scores {1}; on oxygen scores {2}; systolic BP 98 scores {3}; pulse 112 scores {4}; new confusion scores {5}; temperature 38.4 °C scores {6}. His total NEWS2 is {7}, which means {8}.

options: urgent review within 30 minutes
an emergency response (rapid response team)

items.q: Highlight the changes since 22:00 that show Walter is deteriorating.
items.rationale: Worsening mentation, breathing, oxygenation, blood pressure, heart rate and urine output over 4 hours indicate deterioration, probably sepsis from pneumonia. Rusty sputum is consistent with his known pneumonia, and the allergy is not a change.
options: New confusion and pulling at his oxygen
Respiratory rate 20 → 26 with accessory muscle use
SpO₂ 94% → 91% on the same oxygen
Systolic BP 128 → 98 mm Hg
Heart rate 96 → 112
Urine 100 mL in 4 hours
Rusty sputum
Clarithromycin allergy

items.q: Place each statement in the correct part of an SBAR.
items.rationale: Situation states who and the immediate problem; Background gives relevant history and treatment; Assessment gives the data and the nurse's interpretation; Recommendation states clearly what is needed and when.
rows: "I'm calling about Walter Brooks in room 7; he is newly confused and his NEWS2 is 16."
"He was admitted yesterday with right lower lobe pneumonia, is on ceftriaxone and doxycycline, and has mild COPD."
"RR 26, SpO₂ 91% on 2 L, BP 98/60 down from 128/76, HR 112, temperature 38.4, urine 100 mL in 4 hours. I think he may be septic."
"I need you to see him now. Should I call the rapid response team, and may I get a lactate and blood cultures?"

items.q: Dr. Benson says, "Turn up the oxygen and keep an eye on him; I'm busy in the ED." What should the nurse do now?
items.rationale: A NEWS2 of 16 requires an emergency response regardless of the resident's availability, and any nurse may call the rapid response team for concern. When a concern is not addressed, the nurse escalates through the chain of command (charge nurse, rapid response, attending). Delaying risks preventable harm.
options: Increase the oxygen and recheck in 4 hours as he said
Wait until the attending's morning rounds
Call the rapid response team per policy (NEWS2 ≥ 7), stay with the patient, and notify the charge nurse
Call Mrs. Brooks to ask her to come in and decide

items.q: Which communication practices help keep Walter safe? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Read-back, CUS language, closed-loop communication, clear documentation and structured handover are TeamSTEPPS tools that prevent communication failures. Speaking up for patient safety is a professional responsibility.
options: Read back verbal orders and confirm them with the prescriber
Use a "stop the line" phrase from the CUS approach ("I am concerned, I am uncomfortable, this is a safety issue")
Document the times of calls, who was called, what was said and the response
Avoid challenging a physician's decision because it may damage the relationship
Restate the plan and expected timings at the end of the call (closed-loop communication)
Hand over to the rapid response team with a brief SBAR when they arrive

items.q: Put the nurse's actions at 02:15 in order.
items.rationale: Immediate patient support comes first (his own SpO₂ target is 94-98%, as he does not retain CO₂), then the emergency call and the charge nurse. Structured handover and safe implementation of orders follow, with notification of the attending and accurate documentation.
options: Give SBAR to the rapid response team and carry out new orders with read-back
Notify the attending physician as policy requires and document the event, including the earlier call
Call the rapid response team
Stay with Walter, raise the head of the bed, increase oxygen to reach 94-98% and reapply it
Notify the charge nurse

items.q: After the rapid response, Walter is transferred to step-down with sepsis. Reflect: what could have helped the 02:05 call succeed? Write the SBAR you wish you had given, including a clear, time-bound recommendation.
items.rationale: Credit reflection on structure, trend data, explicit concern, policy and escalation, and an SBAR with a time-bound, specific recommendation.
items.model: What could help: lead with the NEWS2 score and "new confusion" in the first sentence; compare with the 22:00 values to show the trend; state an explicit concern ("I think he may be septic"); make a specific, time-bound request; use CUS language if dismissed; know the policy (NEWS2 ≥ 7 requires an emergency response); involve the charge nurse early. SBAR: "Dr. Benson, this is [name], RN on 4 East. I'm concerned about Walter Brooks in room 7: NEWS2 has gone from 4 at 22:00 to 16 now, with new confusion. He was admitted yesterday with right lower lobe pneumonia on ceftriaxone and doxycycline, with mild COPD. RR 26 with accessory muscles, SpO₂ 91% on 2 L, BP 98/60 from 128/76, HR 112, temperature 38.4, only 100 mL urine in 4 hours. I think he is developing sepsis and possibly respiratory failure. I need you to see him within the next 15 minutes; with a NEWS2 of 16, policy requires me to call the rapid response team now, and I am doing that. Can I draw a lactate and blood cultures and give a fluid bolus while we wait? I will read back the orders."

cases.title: Case 32: Five Patients, One Shift: Delegation and Prioritization on a Busy Unit
cases.short: Five Patients, One Shift: Delegation and Prioritization on a Busy Unit
cases.description: You have five patients on a medical-surgical unit, an LPN and a nursing assistant. Decide whom to see first, what to delegate to whom, and how to communicate a clear delegation.
objectives: Prioritize among several patients using ABCs, stability and urgency.
Apply the five rights of delegation and scope of practice for RNs, LPNs/LVNs and assistive personnel.
Give a complete delegation with specific instructions and reporting parameters.
Resolve a delegation conflict professionally.
cases.scenario: It is 07:15. You are the RN for five patients (see the assignment board in Documents). You work with Ana, an LPN, and Marcus, a nursing assistant. Your patient in this chart, Gloria Mendes, is one of them.

items.q: Rank the five patients in the order you should assess them.
items.rationale: An acute change in breathing (airway and breathing, unstable) comes first. A diabetic patient going to surgery soon is time-sensitive (glucose and safety checklist). Uncontrolled pain affects recovery and mobility. A stable patient with chronic needs follows, and a stable patient being discharged is last (discharge teaching can be scheduled).
options: Room 12, Mrs. Mendes: pain 6/10 with oxycodone due; fall risk
Room 15, Mrs. Clarke: stable stroke patient needing assisted feeding
Room 10, Mr. Diaz: SpO₂ 86% and tripoding, worse than at 04:00
Room 11, Ms. Hall: surgery at 09:00, needs glucose check, checklist and antibiotic
Room 14, Mr. Yamamoto: stable, going home today

items.q: Assign each task to the most appropriate team member (assume a state where LPNs give oral and subcutaneous medications and reinforce teaching).
items.rationale: Assessment of unstable patients, initial teaching and pre-operative verification require RN judgment. LPNs can give oral and subcutaneous medications and remove peripheral IVs for stable patients (within state scope and agency policy). Assistive personnel can feed a stable patient whose swallowing has been assessed and plan written (the RN monitors), assist with mobility and toileting, and measure vital signs.
rows: Assess Mr. Diaz's worsening respiratory status
Give Mrs. Mendes's oxycodone and enoxaparin
Feed Mrs. Clarke her breakfast using the dysphagia precautions in her plan
Initial discharge teaching for Mr. Yamamoto
Help Mrs. Mendes to the bathroom and record vital signs
Complete the pre-op assessment and verify Ms. Hall's readiness for surgery

items.q: Complete the five rights of delegation.
items.rationale: The NCSBN and ANA five rights are: right task, circumstance, person, directions and communication, and supervision and evaluation. The RN keeps accountability for delegated care and cannot delegate the nursing process functions that require judgment.
items.text: The five rights are the right {0}, the right circumstance, the right {1}, the right directions and communication, and the right {2}. Tasks that require {3} cannot be delegated to assistive personnel.

time

items.q: Which instructions to Marcus are complete and appropriate? Select all that apply.
items.rationale: Clear delegation states the task, how to do it, the time frame, and specific findings to report, and checks understanding. "See if he seems okay" requires assessment of an unstable patient (an RN task), and assessing swallowing is an RN (or speech therapist) responsibility.
options: "Please take Mrs. Mendes's vital signs now and tell me right away if her systolic BP is below 100 or above 160, her heart rate is over 110, or her temperature is 38.0 or higher."
"Check on Mr. Diaz and see if he seems okay."
"When you help Mrs. Mendes to the bathroom, use the walker and a gait belt, stay with her, and call me if she is dizzy or her pain is much worse."
"Assess Mrs. Clarke's swallowing before breakfast."
"Feed Mrs. Clarke sitting fully upright, small spoonfuls of the thickened diet, and stop and call me if she coughs, chokes or her voice sounds wet."
"Can you repeat back what you will report to me?"

items.q: Marcus says, "I don't have time to feed Mrs. Clarke; that's not my job." What is the RN's best response?
items.rationale: Addressing the concern directly and respectfully, and problem-solving workload together, maintains teamwork and patient safety. Taking over everything is not sustainable, threats escalate conflict, and handing a dysphagia patient's feeding to an untrained visitor is unsafe without assessment and teaching.
options: "Fine, I'll do it myself."
"If you don't do it, I'll report you to the manager."
"It sounds like your morning is really full. Let's look at your tasks together and see what I can rearrange so Mrs. Clarke gets fed safely within the hour."
Ask the patient's daughter to feed her instead

items.q: At 07:20 you are with Mr. Diaz (SpO₂ 88% after repositioning; the respiratory therapist is coming). Ms. Hall's surgery is at 09:00. What is the best way to manage her time-sensitive needs?
items.rationale: The RN stays with the unstable patient while delegating appropriate parts of the pre-operative work to the LPN, then completes the assessment and verification that require RN judgment. If the workload threatens safety, the charge nurse can help. Assistive personnel cannot verify consent or complete the RN checklist.
options: Ask Marcus to complete her pre-op checklist and verify the consent
Ask Ana to check her glucose and gather the checklist items, and complete the pre-op assessment and verification yourself as soon as Mr. Diaz is stabilized; call the charge nurse if you cannot
Call the operating room to cancel her surgery
Leave Mr. Diaz to finish Ms. Hall's checklist

items.q: Write the delegation you would give Ana (LPN) for Mrs. Mendes this morning, using the five rights, including what you want reported and when you will follow up.
items.rationale: Credit a delegation within LPN scope, with specific tasks and times, clear report parameters, fall precautions, a follow-up time and a check of understanding.
items.model: "Ana, could you take Mrs. Mendes in 12 this morning? She is POD 1 after a left knee replacement and is stable. Please give her oxycodone 5-10 mg now for pain 6/10, reassess her pain in about an hour, and give her enoxaparin at 09:00. Check her left leg neurovascular status (color, warmth, capillary refill, sensation, movement) with her vital signs at 09:00. She is a fall risk: bed alarm on, and two people or the walker with a gait belt for the bathroom. She has her first walk with PT at 10:00, so please make sure her pain is controlled before then. Tell me right away if her pain is still 6 or more an hour after the oxycodone, if her toes are cool, pale or numb, if her calf is swollen or painful, if she is short of breath, or if her vital signs change (systolic BP below 100, HR above 110). I'll check in with you at 08:30 and see her myself after Mr. Diaz is stable. Does that work for you? Can you tell me what you'll report?"

cases.title: Case 33: Breaking the Chain: Clostridioides difficile and Infection Prevention
cases.short: Breaking the Chain: Clostridioides difficile and Infection Prevention
cases.description: A 72-year-old man on antibiotics and a proton pump inhibitor develops profuse diarrhea and tests positive for C. difficile. Implement the right precautions, catch an unsafe practice, and teach his family.
objectives: Recognize risk factors and signs of Clostridioides difficile infection, including severe disease.
Implement contact precautions and correct hand hygiene for spore-forming organisms.
Identify and correct unsafe infection-prevention practices.
Teach patients and visitors to prevent transmission.
cases.scenario: You are the nurse on the medical unit. Vincent Russo's stool test has just come back positive. His wife is visiting, and a student nurse has just finished helping him to the commode.

items.q: Highlight Vincent's risk factors for C. difficile infection.
items.rationale: Antibiotics (especially clindamycin and broad-spectrum agents) disrupt normal gut flora; PPIs, older age and hospitalization increase risk, and shared rooms and bathrooms increase exposure. His occupation and lack of allergies are unrelated.
options: Clindamycin and then piperacillin-tazobactam for a week
Long-term pantoprazole (proton pump inhibitor)
Age 72
Hospital stay of 7 days
Retired baker
Shares a room and bathroom
Allergic to nothing

items.q: For each finding, decide whether it indicates severe C. difficile infection or is a general finding.
items.rationale: Severe infection is defined by a WBC of 15,000 or more or a creatinine above 1.5 mg/dL. Hypotension, shock, ileus or megacolon indicate fulminant disease. Diarrhea and cramps are typical of any C. difficile infection.
rows: Hypotension, ileus or a markedly distended abdomen (if they developed)

items.q: The student nurse used alcohol-based hand rub after helping Vincent to the commode. What should you tell her?
items.rationale: C. difficile spores resist alcohol. Gloves are the main protection, and soap and water with friction removes spores mechanically. Bleach is used on surfaces, never on skin.
options: "That's fine; alcohol rub is the best hand hygiene in all situations."
"For C. difficile, wash with soap and water after removing your gloves. Alcohol does not kill the spores; washing physically removes them."
"You only need hand hygiene if you touched the stool."
"Use a bleach wipe on your hands."

items.q: Classify each practice as correct or incorrect for Vincent's care.
items.rationale: Contact plus precautions need dedicated equipment, sporicidal cleaning and a private room or dedicated toilet. Antimotility agents such as loperamide are avoided in active C. difficile infection (risk of toxic megacolon) unless specifically approved by the provider. PPIs and unnecessary antibiotics should be reviewed and stopped if possible.
rows: Put on a gown and gloves before entering the room
Use the shared hallway blood pressure cuff and return it to the hallway
Clean surfaces with a sporicidal (bleach-based) disinfectant
Give the loperamide ordered on admission for the loose stools
Move him to a private room with his own bathroom when available, or dedicate a commode now

items.q: Put the nurse's actions in priority order.
items.rationale: Preventing transmission starts immediately, alongside treatment of the infection and dehydration. Stopping harmful or unnecessary drugs comes next, then environmental control and exposure follow-up, and teaching completes the plan (and continues throughout).
options: Start contact plus precautions now: dedicated commode and equipment, gown and gloves, a precaution sign on the door
Teach Vincent and Rosa about hand washing, precautions and laundry
Give the first dose of oral vancomycin and continue IV fluids for dehydration
Hold the PRN loperamide and ask the provider to review the pantoprazole and antibiotics
Arrange the private room transfer and terminal bleach cleaning of the shared bathroom; notify the roommate's team

items.q: Complete the nurse's explanation to the student.
items.rationale: Spores persist in the environment and are transmitted by contact. Oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin act in the gut lumen; IV vancomycin does not reach the colon in useful amounts (IV metronidazole may be added only in fulminant disease).
items.text: C. difficile forms {0} that can survive on surfaces for {1}. It is spread by the {2} route, mostly on the hands of staff and on shared equipment. Treatment of the infection is with {3}, because the drug must reach the colon.

options: spores
cysts
hours
months
airborne
fecal-oral (contact)
oral vancomycin or fidaxomicin
intravenous vancomycin

items.q: Rosa sits on the bed, brings food daily, wants to take his laundry home, and her 18-month-old grandchild visits on weekends. Write the teaching you would give her, in plain language.
items.rationale: Credit accurate, practical advice on PPE and soap-and-water hand hygiene, sitting and bathroom use, laundry, food, young visitors and home cleaning, with teach-back.
items.model: "Vincent has an infection in his bowel called C. diff. The germ spreads through tiny spores in his stool that can stay on surfaces and hands. You can keep visiting. Please put on a gown and gloves when you come in, and when you leave, take them off in the room and wash your hands with soap and water for at least 20 seconds; the hand gel does not kill this germ. Please sit in the chair rather than on his bed, and don't use his bathroom. You can bring food that he is allowed to eat, in containers you won't take back home, and take the empty bag out after washing your hands. For laundry, put it straight into a plastic bag, wash it separately on the hottest setting the fabric allows with detergent (and bleach where safe), and wash your hands afterward. It's best if young children don't visit while he has diarrhea; when he goes home, everyone should wash hands with soap and water after using the toilet and before eating, and the bathroom should be cleaned with a bleach-based cleaner." Check understanding with teach-back.

P01.name: Hana Kareem
P01.reason: Intrauterine fetal demise at 37 weeks 2 days; induced vaginal delivery of a stillborn male at 03:12
alerts: Perinatal loss: bereavement door card in place
P01.summary: G3 P2011. Presented with no fetal movement for about 24 hours. No fetal heart tones; ultrasound confirmed fetal demise. Induced with misoprostol; spontaneous vaginal delivery of a stillborn male (2,840 g) at 03:12. Second-degree laceration repaired. EBL 450 mL.

narratives.title: Handoff report
narratives.speaker: Grace, night shift RN
narratives.text:
This is Hana Kareem in room 6, she's 39, G3 now P2011. She came in last evening because she hadn't felt the baby move for about a day, and we couldn't find heart tones. Ultrasound confirmed a fetal demise at 37 and 2. She was induced with misoprostol and delivered a stillborn boy at 03:12. His name is Yusuf. Second-degree lac, repaired. Estimated blood loss was 450.

She came over to us around five. Her husband Omar has been with her all night. They held Yusuf for a little while after delivery and then asked us to take him to the nursery cooler. They haven't decided about photos or footprints yet. Omar asked me twice about an imam and about how soon they can take Yusuf for burial, so that still needs to be arranged. I left a message with spiritual care but nobody called back yet.

Physically: at 06:15 her pad was saturated in about an hour and her fundus was boggy. It firmed up with massage, one below the umbilicus, and the oxytocin infusion is still running. I haven't rechecked since. Vitals have been stable, heart rate went up to 96 at that check. Pain is 3 out of 10, cramping, she had ibuprofen at 04:00.

She's O negative. The cord blood type is pending and the Kleihauer-Betke is pending, so the RhoGAM hasn't been given yet.

Emotionally, she's very quiet. She keeps saying it's her fault, that she should have come in sooner. She's a pharmacist, so she's asking a lot of questions about why this happened. The autopsy consent conversation is today with Dr. Morgan. She has a history of anxiety after a miscarriage in 2023. She hasn't slept. Their six-year-old is at home with grandma and they're worried about what to tell her.

narratives.text:
Next is Mr. Al-Harbi, 52, type 2 diabetes for eleven years. He's on metformin 1000 twice a day, glimepiride 4 milligrams in the morning, and glargine 24 units at bedtime. His A1c is 8.1, down from 8.9. eGFR is 72.

I'm planning to move the glimepiride to iftar and drop it to 2 milligrams, and reduce the glargine by about 20 percent and give it at iftar. Metformin stays the same total, at iftar and suhoor. Can you go through glucose monitoring, when to break the fast, hypoglycemia, and meals with him? His wife cooks; she's coming in too. He's a respected man in his mosque and he told me he doesn't want to be told not to fast.

Her baseline blood pressure is low, about 90s over 60, heart rate 60s. She gets dizzy when we sit her up fast, so we use the abdominal binder and compression stockings.

Emotionally, she's quiet. She was on the swim team and she was supposed to go to prom next month. She asked me last night if she'll ever walk again. Mom is here most of the time and is very anxious, she wants to do everything for her.

She has PT and OT all morning, then a psychology session at one. Her next cath is due at 11:30.

Miriam Feldman in 2, 77, metastatic pancreatic cancer. She had a family meeting yesterday with palliative care and her daughter Rachel, who's her health care proxy. Miriam herself said two weeks ago, while she could still talk, that she doesn't want to be on machines, and she has a living will that says no CPR, no ventilator, no feeding tube. She's comfort-focused now: DNR, DNI.

Today she's mostly unresponsive, she opens her eyes to her name briefly. Her breathing has a pattern, fast and deep then pauses up to 20 seconds. There's a rattling sound with each breath. Her knees and feet are mottled and cool. Urine's only been about 60 for the whole shift, dark.

She's on a morphine infusion at 1 milligram an hour with boluses; she had a bolus at 21:00 when she was grimacing and breathing fast. She has glycopyrrolate ordered for the secretions; I haven't given it yet.

Her son Daniel flew in today from Israel; he hadn't seen her since summer and he's shocked. He's asking for everything to be done, the ICU, a feeding tube. Rachel is exhausted and in tears; they argued in the hallway. The family would like the rabbi to come; they're asking about what happens after she dies, they want her body to be handled according to Jewish tradition and buried quickly.

narratives.title: Midday update
narratives.speaker: Charge nurse
narratives.text:
Vincent Russo in 16A, 72, in for a diabetic foot infection, he's been on clindamycin and then piperacillin-tazobactam for a week. He's on pantoprazole too. Since yesterday he's had seven or eight watery stools, foul-smelling, with cramping. Temp 38.3. The C. diff toxin just came back positive.

His roommate in bed B is 84 and on antibiotics for pneumonia. We're trying to get Mr. Russo a private room; one should open this afternoon.

I saw the student nurse come out of the room and use the alcohol foam on her hands, she didn't wash with soap and water. The shared blood pressure cuff from the hallway is in his room. Housekeeping uses the regular disinfectant wipes.

His wife Rosa brings him food every day and sits on his bed. She asked if she can take his laundry home. His creatinine bumped up today, and his white count is high.
